en: The Śramaṇa Fǎbǎo has composed this work and will now explain this treatise through a fivefold analysis: first, the initial turning of the wheel of Dharma;
second, the sequence of study and practice; third, the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching; fourth, the chronological order of the various sectarian tenets; and fifth, based on...
Explanation of the Text: Regarding "at the time of the first turning of the wheel of Dharma in the first assembly," there are four parts.
First, the determination of the day of attaining enlightenment.
1. The day of turning the wheel of Dharma;
2. The day of attaining enlightenment; 3. A detailed account of intermediate events;
4. A reconciliation of differing accounts. Regarding the first, the day of attaining enlightenment:
According to the fourth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, it is said:
"On the eighth day the Tathāgata was born;
on the eighth day the Buddha left the household life."
On the eighth day he attained enlightenment;
on the eighth day he entered parinirvāṇa. The subsequent passage states:
"In the second month, the Tathāgata was born."
In the second month the Buddha left home;
in the second month he attained enlightenment;
in the second month he entered nirvana. Furthermore, the *Guanfo jing* (Sutra on Contemplating the Buddha) states:
The Buddha told the devas and humans:
"The Buddhas of the ten directions are all born at midnight on the eighth day of the fourth month."
All went forth into homelessness at midnight on the eighth day of the fourth month;
all attained enlightenment at midnight on the eighth day of the fourth month;
all [performed this] at midnight on the eighth day of the fourth month.
He entered parinirvāṇa;
while the eighth day is the same across all sūtras,
the months mentioned differ.
There are only two [positions], differing in four ways;
it does not mention other months. Based on the two explanations above, although the formulations differ, [the meaning remains consistent].
The month and day of his attainment of enlightenment are identical.
This can be known through two general principles.
First, because they establish the beginning of the year differently:
in the country of the Brahmins, the year begins with the month of Jiazi (the eleventh lunar month),
whereas in this region, it was previously established that the year begins with the month of Jiating (the first lunar month).
The fourth month of the *jianzi* [lunar calendar] is equivalent to the second month of the *jianti*. Therefore,
those who preserve the Sanskrit original refer to it as the fourth month.
Regarding this region, it is said that [the month] is the second;
the fundamental [reckoning] is one. Second, according to the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* and the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, the calculation is as follows.
The Brahma King requested him to come forth fifty-seven days prior;
for four months he refined his faculties while simultaneously observing the capacities of beings, totaling six months,
which corresponds to his attainment of enlightenment on the eighth day of the second month.
On the eighth day of the eighth month, he entered the samādhi of turning the wheel of Dharma,
as indicated by the following cited passage. From this, it is known.
It is established that he attained enlightenment on the eighth day of the second month,
as there are six months remaining until the eighth day of the eighth month;
if it were the eighth day of the fourth month, [the calculation would not hold].
Thus, there are no six months;
it is four months prior to the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, as there is no textual evidence [to the contrary]. Furthermore, the Vinaya-śāstra explains:
The Buddha, together with five bhikṣus,
entered the *pūrvavarṣā* (the first retreat) on the sixteenth day of the fourth month;
the retreat began on the eighth day of the fourth month.
There were only nine days remaining.
He then bestowed upon him numerous sutras and treatises, such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, and the *Vibhāṣā*,
which were as vast as the sun and moon.
Based on this, it is known that the eighth day of the second month is established as the date of his attainment of enlightenment. Question:
If this is so, why does the *Bodhisattva-cchatra-sūtra* state:
It is said that on the eighth day of the second month he attained enlightenment;
on the eighth day of the second month he turned the wheel of Dharma;
and on the eighth day of the second month he subdued Māra.
Regarding the statement that [the Buddha] entered parinirvāṇa on the eighth day of the second month, there are two explanations for this. First,
the *Cūtīgarbha-sūtra* states that while the Bodhisattva was dwelling in the womb, he also turned the wheel of Dharma.
This refers to the assembly of bees,
not the assembly of humans.
On the very day he attained enlightenment, he turned the Wheel of Dharma.
The meaning is also to be understood accordingly.
Regarding the current statement that the Wheel of Dharma was turned for the five bhikṣus on a certain day, various accounts differ.
This is not the tradition of the Miṅzhòng (Mūlasarvāstivāda). Furthermore, in various sūtras, there are instances where the second month has been mistakenly recorded as the fourth month.
Regarding the establishment of the correct [calendar],
it has already been explained as before.
As for the error of taking the eighth month as the second month and the fourth month [as the sixth]:
*Kārttika* is the name of the lunar mansion *Mṛgaśiras* (the Rabbit) in the eighth month;
the second month is likewise the month when the earth is established in the *mṛga* (rabbit) position.
Thus, the asterism and the earth are distinguished by their respective designations.
The name "Mao" (卯) signifies "sameness.
If one knows that Kārttika is the Mao of the western direction (West), it corresponds to the eighth month.
If one considers Kārttika to be the Mao of the eastern direction (East), [it would correspond to the second month].
Translated, these become the second and fourth months;
thus, due to the dates for turning the wheel of Dharma and other such events,
there are differences of two, four, or eight days.
Regarding the date of the Parinirvāṇa,
there are differences among the traditions of the eighth, fourth, and second months;
this is detailed in many teachings and principles.
The conversion of the five bhikṣus is fixed at eight months [after the enlightenment].
The date of the assembly on the day of the Parinirvāṇa is explained in a separate chapter.
Second, regarding the date of the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, all the sūtras and śāstras state:
In the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī,
he turned the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths for the five bhikṣus;
regarding the intermediate events, the accounts differ as to the number of days.
However, as for not specifying the date, month, day, or name when citing the teachings,
one cannot rely on that alone;
it must be verified against the *Mahāvibhāṣā* and the commentaries on the Vinaya.
The specific dates on which these teachings were expounded are clearly indicated;
one should rely upon this text.
The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 183, states:
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika,
the Buddha ordained Ājñātakauṇḍinya. Kārttika.
This corresponds to the eighth month of this region.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 136, states:
"On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, day and night are equal; by the ninth day, the night increases by one *nāḍī*."
Although the terms *kaṭha* and *kāṭhaka* differ, their meaning is the same;
therefore, it is known that this must certainly be the eighth day of the eighth month.
Furthermore, the Vinaya-śāstra states:
On the sixteenth day of the fourth month, the Buddha entered the preceding *anuvāsa* (rainy season retreat) together with the five bhikṣus.
During the entire summer retreat, he did not attain the fruit of sainthood;
however, after the retreat had passed, on the eighth day of the eighth month,
Kauṇḍinya suddenly realized the Dharma.
The reasoning in these two treatises is extremely clear, whereas the other texts are not; therefore, they cannot be relied upon as authoritative.
Thus, it is known that the turning of the Wheel of Dharma was definitively on the eighth day of the eighth month.
Although there are two differing accounts regarding the date of the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment—
either the eighth day of the second month or the eighth day of the fourth month.
Since neither the sūtras nor the śāstras state that the Wheel of Dharma was turned in the second or fourth month,
we know it did not occur thirty-seven days later.
Furthermore, there are no texts stating it occurred in the third, fourth, fifth, or sixth month.

Thus we know that it was not after six or seven days, nor eight or seven days, nor fifty-seven days, that the Wheel of Dharma was turned. Third, regarding the specific account of events during the intervening period:
within the Sūtras, Vinayas, and Śāstras...
The accounts of the period between attaining enlightenment and turning the wheel of Dharma differ in their degree of detail;
there are discrepancies between the earlier and later versions.
For now, we shall first examine the period prior to the observation of capacities,
as narrated according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*; following that,
we shall examine the period after the observation of capacities.
According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, the remaining textual variations are recorded here in sequence. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, fascicle 31, states:
"During the first watch of the night, one attains the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*)."
In the middle watch of the night, he attained the clear knowledge of death and rebirth;
in the latter watch of the night, he attained the clear knowledge of the destruction of the outflows.
Having attained these three types of clear knowledge, [he became an Arhat].
He immediately went beneath the Bodhi tree,
sat down cross-legged,
and for seven days remained unmoving, experiencing the bliss of liberation.
After seven days had passed, he arose from that meditative absorption and accepted parched grain and honey from two merchant brothers,
granting them the two refuges.
It is said that this was the first time such a lay follower (upāsaka) appeared.
The Four Heavenly Kings offered alms bowls for him to receive the parched grain and honey;
this was the first seven-day period.
The *Kāraṇaprajñapti-sūtra* states that after observing the capacities of sentient beings, [the Buddha] accepted the flour and honey from a merchant. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* says:
"Having eaten the flour and honey, he sat beneath a tree in the full lotus posture for seven days without moving."
Wandering in the liberation-samādhi, after seven days had passed, he arose from that samādhi.
Not far from there was a tree bearing harītakī fruits.
Thereupon, the tree deity offered a harītakī fruit to the World-Honored One.
Having accepted it, he conferred the two refuges upon her.
This was the second seven-day period. Having eaten this fruit, he entered meditative concentration as before.
Emerging from meditative absorption, he entered the village of Uruvilvā to beg for alms.
Having accepted food from a brāhmaṇa, he granted him the two refuges.
This was the third seven-day period. Thus, the above three weeks were spent beneath the Bodhi tree. After eating, he proceeded once more to the foot of an Ālamba tree.
As before, he entered meditative concentration.
Having emerged from concentration, he entered the village of Uruvilvā to beg for food and accepted an offering of food from the wife of a brahmin.
He conferred the two refuges upon her,
saying, "This is the beginning of [the status of] an upāsikā. According to this Vinaya text,
a person receives the upāsaka precepts by receiving the three refuges.
"Your Majesty, this is not so.
It is the fourth seven-day period. Having finished eating, he returned to the foot of the Līpāvana tree and entered meditative concentration as before.
Having arisen from meditative concentration, he entered the village of Uruvilvā to beg for alms,
receiving food from Brahmin men and women.
He conferred the Three Refuges upon him.
This was the fifth seven-day period.
During the preceding two seven-day periods, he stayed beneath the Līvanā tree; after eating, he went to the palace of the Dragon King Manasvin.
Having arrived, he entered meditative absorption as before.
It rained for seven days;
even until the seventh week, the Dragon King encircled the Buddha’s head with his body to shield the Buddha from above.

The *Kāraṇaprajñapti-sūtra* follows the section on "Observing the Capabilities. Above, [it describes] the sixth and seventh [stages]: receiving and understanding the bliss of the samādhi of liberation. Furthermore, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"Having arisen from meditative concentration, he went to the foot of the Aśvattha tree in Nyagrodhavana."
He spread out his sitting mat and sat in the full lotus posture. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"He entered samādhi for seven days. It further states:
"He received the curd as if a person were eating it."
Having finished eating, he entered meditative concentration.
The above is from the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*. Furthermore, the *Caturvargika-vinaya* says:
He formed this thought, saying:
I have now attained this Dharma, which is extremely profound,
difficult to understand, and difficult to know;
I wish for tranquility and rest.
This subtle and supreme [truth] can be known by those of wisdom.
Having reflected upon it, he spoke two verses;
having spoken the two verses, he remained silent. This concludes the period of reflecting on the profound Dharma.
It does not specify the number of days; the *Lotus Sūtra* states:
"He contemplated the trees and also practiced walking meditation for twenty-one days."
Reflecting upon these matters,
I have attained wisdom that is subtle, profound, and supreme.
Sentient beings have dull faculties;
attached to pleasure and blinded by ignorance,
such as these are their kind.
How can one be delivered? This is consistent with the intent of the Vinaya; it follows the preceding [text].
For six or seven days, one experiences the bliss of liberation;
for three or seven days, one contemplates the Dharma.
In total, there are nine weeks;
the day of emergence from meditative absorption is the first day of the subsequent seven-day period.
This excludes the six days of repetition.
There remain fifty-seven days. During this time,
the Brahma King requested [the Buddha] to grant him the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* and the *Vibhāṣā*.
The number of days is the same.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle eight, states:
"After Śākyamuni Buddha attained the Way..."
"For fifty-seven days, why did you not preach the Dharma?
You said that my Dharma is extremely profound, difficult to understand, and difficult to know;
that all sentient beings are bound and attached to worldly dharmas and none are able to comprehend it."
"It would be better to remain silent and enter parinirvāṇa in bliss.
At that time, Brahmā Śikhin and others entreated the Buddha to turn the Wheel of Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings for the first time.
The Buddha—
At that time, he accepted the invitation by remaining silent.

Later, he went to the forest of Vārāṇasī and turned the Wheel of the True Dharma; this is in agreement with the intent of the *Vinaya* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Furthermore, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
The Brahma King requested the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma;
having granted his consent, the Buddha, the Brahma King returned to his palace. The above constitutes the observation of capacities (*tatkāla-avalokana*).
This general meaning is the same as that found in the *Vinaya* and the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
The minor differences in the interim are omitted for brevity. The above is based on the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 182, which states:
"When the Bodhisattva was beneath the Bodhi tree..."
In his thirty-fourth thought-moment, he attained unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
With the Buddha-eye, he surveyed all worlds to see who should be the first to hear his true Dharma.
"I shall explain it for you;
once you have contemplated it, you will understand.
The son of Rāṇamati should first hear my Dharma."
At that time, a deva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The son of Yaśoda passed away last night.
Some say it was seven days ago; the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
Udraka Rāmaputra passed away seven days later. Furthermore, it is said:
at that time, the World-Honored One also gave rise to wisdom and vision and knew that he had reached the end of his life.
He then uttered a sigh of lamentation, saying:
"They have lost a great benefit.
Had they heard the Dharma I preached, [they would not have fallen into such a state]."
He will attain right understanding.
The World-Honored One further observed who else,
besides him, should first hear my True Dharma.
"I shall explain it for you;
once you have observed it, you will know.
Thus says the *Aṅgulimāla-sūtra* in its fourth fascicle.
"Āḷāra Kālāma should have been the first to hear the Dharma.
The deva further addressed the Buddha, saying:
"He passed away seven days ago. Some say it was yesterday; the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* also states it was yesterday. At that time, the World-Honored One...
He also gives rise to wisdom and vision, knowing their faults.
As before, he utters a lamentation. [The Buddha] asks: "When one first attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi..."
"Why did you not preach the Dharma to these two individuals?
Since they have passed away without hearing the Dharma, has the Tathāgata’s teaching not missed its opportune time? Furthermore, it says:
At that time, the roots of goodness of those two were not yet matured,
and they were not yet capable of hearing the Dharma. Why was this?
After the Buddha had attained enlightenment,
if that first person still had more than fifty-seven days remaining of their life, [he would have been saved].
He should be capable of hearing the Dharma.
As for that second person,
if he has more than fifty-one days remaining of his life, [he too is capable].
They should be capable of hearing the Dharma;
for this reason, there would be the fault of the Buddha’s teaching being untimely.
According to this treatise, although the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* does not explain in detail the number of days prior to the Brahmā King’s request, [the meaning is as stated].
However, with the exception of the day the Buddha attained enlightenment,
up until the fifty-seventh day prior to his permitted departure [from this world], it is the same as in the Vinaya and the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*. Furthermore,
it is said that the World-Honored One sometimes retained his life-force (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*).
As in the case of Subhadra and others;
if it were so that one could preserve the life-force of another, such a thing would be impossible.
According to this treatise, [it is not possible].
"I shall not withhold the life-span from others.
The Blessed One further reflected: "Setting aside those two individuals, who is the first who ought to hear my teaching of the Dharma?"
"I shall explain it for you;
upon contemplation, you will immediately understand.
Kauṇḍinya and the other four should first hear the Dharma."
He then thought to himself:
"They were all my parents and kinsmen;
in the past, they have always shown me respect and made offerings to me."
"Now, where is he whom I wish to repay his kindness?
The deva immediately replied,
"He is currently in the Deer Park of the Rishis in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī."
At that time, the World-Honored One also gave rise to knowledge and vision, knowing that he was there;
he then left beneath the Bodhi tree and proceeded on foot toward him.
Question: Since the Buddha possesses the most supreme supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), for what reason does he travel on foot?
Answer: Out of reverence for the Dharma, he does not employ his supernormal powers.
Furthermore, when the Buddha walks, his feet are always four finger-widths (*catur-aṅgula*) above the ground.
Each footprint was clearly marked with the auspicious and lovely thousand-spoked wheel sign (*sahasrāra-cakra*), complete with joyous swirls (*nandyāvarta*) as distinct as a painting;
wherever his shadow touched the ground, it remained so for seven days.
Those sentient beings who were able to reach that place had their faculties become peaceful and refreshed.
Gradually proceeding on their journey, they arrived at Vārāṇasī.
At that time...
The five men suddenly encountered the Buddha and immediately established a pact among themselves:
"As for that Gautama..."
Lax and seeking much,
they are deranged and lose mindfulness;
in vain, they obtain nothing.
Now they have come again, wishing to summon and entice us.
We should each ignore them in speech, neither showing them respect nor exchanging greetings;
we should simply prepare a single ordinary seat for them.
"Is he sitting? At that time,
the World-Honored One gradually drew near him,
overwhelmed by his majestic power.
Causing him to abandon his original intention,
he unconsciously rose from his seat all at once,
ran forward to meet him, joined his palms, and took refuge in him.
Among them,
some rearranged the pure seats,
while others took up the Buddha’s robe.
Some took the Buddha's almsbowl;
some offered water for washing;
and some washed his feet.
They both addressed the Buddha, saying,
"We pray that you will please take a seat.
The Buddha then formed this thought:
Such foolish people establish their own restraints only to break them again in an instant.
At that time, the Buddha took his seat and sat down with serene composure.
His majestic radiance was extraordinary,
like Mount Sumeru; eventually, the World-Honored One gradually guided and transformed him, causing him to be subdued.
During the first part of the day,
he taught the Dharma for the sake of two people.
He gave them instructions and guidance,
and sent the other three into the village to beg for alms.
The alms he received were sufficient for six people;
in the afternoon,
he taught the Dharma to three of them.
Having given them instructions and guidance,
he sent the other two into the village to beg for alms.
The food and drink he begged for were sufficient for five people;
because the World-Honored One’s nature was free from eating at improper times,
he thus taught and transformed them for three months.
Some say it was four months;
having caused the roots of goodness of those five men to ripen,
on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika.
The Tathāgata turned the wheel of the true Dharma for them;
at that time, Kauṇḍinya was the first to see the Dharma. Regarding the four different accounts of the preaching [of the Dharma], it is asked:
if it was after the Buddha had attained enlightenment...
Regarding the statement that the Wheel of the True Dharma was turned after six months:
why does the *Udānavarga* and the *Mahāvaipulya-sūtra* state it was seven weeks, while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states it was three weeks?
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the Buddha did not preach the Dharma for fifty-seven days;
according to the *Vaipulya-mahāvyūha-sūtra*, he spent twenty-one days in contemplation and twenty-one days walking in meditation.
The *Caoyin jing* (Sutra on Cause and Effect) states that he gazed at the tree for seven days;
the *Fahua jing* (Lotus Sutra) mentions the practice of gazing at the tree but does not specify the number of days;
the *Sifen lü* (Dharmaguptaka Vinaya) states it was six or seven days.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states seven times seven days;
the *Vibhāṣā* states four months;
furthermore, another sutra speaks of half a year.

Question: "Does it take twelve *yojanas* for one year? Answer: Since ancient times, the masters of the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma have all stated that there are differences in what is seen and heard.
This means that when the Buddha was in the world, his majestic power varied according to the capacities of sentient beings.
Some see him turning the wheel of Dharma many days later;
others see him turning the wheel of Dharma few days later. Now, to explain the Tathāgata correctly:

he does not manifest the eight phases of attaining enlightenment in this manner—showing the presence of father, mother, wife, and son, as well as the dates of his birth, renunciation, and attainment of enlightenment.
Regarding the day the Wheel of Dharma was turned for the five bhikṣus,
the explanations of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are logically consistent;
this is evident in accounts of such matters as walking in meditation (caṅkrama), the distances traveled, and the observation of trees.
There may indeed be differences.
Because the signs and phenomena of a Buddha’s supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) in entering meditative absorption (*samādhi*) are difficult to discern, [one asks] how they can be known.
The answer is that there are briefly five types of examples.
First, because the timing of their appearance differs;
second, because the original texts differ in their sequence and degree of detail;
third, because the lifespan, the sun, and the moon are identical.
Fourth, because there are differences between what is taught earlier and later in the same original text;
fifth, because of errors made by the transmitters.
Due to these five reasons, there are said to be distinctions [in the teachings].
The fundamental matter is the same; the difference lies in the duration of the single undertaking.
In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, "six or seven days" refers to the time for experiencing the bliss of liberation (*vimukti-sukha*);
in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, "twenty-one days" [refers to the same].
When contemplating the Dharma,
one should practice for seven weeks according to the *Chuyao jing* (Udānavarga), the *Zhuangyan jing* (Śrī-sūtra),
and the *Wufen lü* (Pañcavargika-vinaya).
Regarding the period of fifty-seven days during which he contemplated the Dharma:
the Brahma King invited him to come forward.
Regarding the "four months of the *Vāśa*":
this refers to the time when the faculties of the five bhikṣus were being trained;
there are accounts that it lasted for half a year.
"Because of the six months":
that which takes twelve [months] constitutes one year means that it passes through one summer.
Regarding the Vinaya and the *Varṣā-śīla-sūtra*,
since the summer retreat constitutes a year, there are differences between two variant versions in their sequence and degree of detail:
in the Vinaya, the former portion is extensive while the latter is concise.
Previously, when explaining separately the contemplation of the Dharma while experiencing the bliss of liberation, the four-month period of refining the faculties was omitted;
subsequently, the invitation by Brahmā prior to that was also omitted. In the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, the preceding section was likewise omitted.
Thereafter, he extensively explains the four-month period for tuning the faculties.

By cross-referencing these two passages, one knows that six months of days had elapsed before he finally began preaching the Dharma. As for the statement that the days and months of the three births are identical:
Since the dates for the father, mother, wife, son, birth, renunciation, and enlightenment— accomplished through the eight phases— are all said to be identical,
how can there be such a vast discrepancy regarding the day he turned the wheel of Dharma for the five bhikṣus?
Therefore, we know that the fundamental source is the same;

it is merely that the transmissions differ in their detail and brevity, and contain errors. Regarding the fourth point, "the original source is the same, yet there are differences between the earlier and later expositions": this refers to the fact that although the root text is identical, the preceding and succeeding explanations vary.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 182, states:
"Under the Bodhi tree, the Buddha attained unexcelled perfect enlightenment through thirty-four moments of mind.
Thereupon, he surveyed all worlds universally with his Buddha-eye."
Who should be the first to hear my True Dharma?
As in the previously cited passage,
it is according to this principle.
After the Buddha attained enlightenment, he immediately observed the capacities of his disciples.
During this interval, the experiences of receiving and realizing liberation, his contemplation of the Dharma, the invitation by Brahmā, and so forth—were these not indeed present?
How could they have been absent?
Therefore, we know that what is missing in various editions is likewise an abbreviation.
If one were to claim that the *Vibhāṣā* contains differing accounts based on what was seen or heard, [the same applies here].
After attaining enlightenment, he immediately observed the capacities and faculties [of sentient beings].
For this reason, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states in the passage following the previous section:
"Of those, the first person..."
If there were still fifty-seven days remaining after the Buddha attained enlightenment,
he would have been capable of hearing the Dharma; this refers to the period following the Buddha's attainment of enlightenment.
The period up to the observation of the faculties (*indriya*) lasts fifty-seven days,
which is the same as in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*.
Furthermore, the first fascicle of the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states:
At that time, the Bodhisattva left the place of ascetic practice,
went beneath the Bodhi tree,
and sat upon the diamond throne, where he subdued the hosts of Māra.
He immediately attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, Brahmā-rāja and the others all went to the Buddha’s abode and exhorted the World-Honored One to first turn the wheel of Dharma. According to this treatise, [this is the case].
He immediately ceased eating the milk-rice and experienced the bliss of liberation while contemplating the Dharma.
After the Buddha attained enlightenment, he was invited by Brahmā-rāja. If,
according to the *Dharmatā-viniścaya-śāstra*, one were to claim that [the Buddha] did not preach because his personal knowledge and what he had heard differed,
why does the eighth fascicle state that after Śākyamuni Buddha attained the Way...?
For fifty-seven days, he did not preach the Dharma.
At that time, Brahmā and others made their request;
the various textual omissions are as they were in the first fascicle, being abbreviated.

It is not that what was seen and heard differs; rather, there are errors in the five successive translations. For example, the Song edition of the *Bhaiṣajyaguru-sūtra* states "the twenty-four precepts of the Bodhisattva Śraddhā," whereas the Tang and Sui editions state "the four hundred precepts of the Bodhisattva."
In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, each of the six sense faculties possesses twelve hundred merits;
in the *Saddharma-puṇḍarīka-sūtra*, three faculties possess twelve hundred merits.
The three faculties [of faith, vigor, and mindfulness] amount to eight hundred, and so forth;
the remaining [faculties] differ and cannot be reconciled with these figures.
All cases are of this same category.
The fundamental principle is one;
it is only because the lineages of transmission differ that there are two.
Second, regarding the sequence of study and practice:
All myriad practices take hearing the Dharma and drawing near to virtuous friends as their beginning.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 25, states:
"All sentient beings, by means of the causal condition of listening to the Dharma..."
They shall draw near to Great Nirvana.
Because all sentient beings listen to the Dharma,
they will possess the faculty of faith.
Because one has attained the faculty of faith,

one delights in practicing generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, thereby attaining the fruit of *srotāpanna*, up to and including the fruit of Buddhahood.
Therefore, one should know that the attainment of all wholesome dharmas is due to the power of the causes and conditions of hearing the Dharma. It is further said:
"Faith arises from hearing the Dharma."
Listening to the Dharma depends upon faith.
Thus, these two factors are both causes and conditions for causes, as well as effects and conditions for effects.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (Treatise on Following Right Reasoning), fascicle 58, states:
The conduct and practices cultivated on the stage of initial application are extremely numerous and extensive.
Those who wish to understand them thoroughly should seek them within the various treatises on contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) accumulated by sentient beings.
In brief, a beginner practitioner should possess a profound aspiration for liberation.
Contemplating the virtues of nirvana and turning away from the faults of saṃsāra,
one should first employ skillful means to draw near to virtuous friends,
for virtuous friends are the foundation of all spiritual practices.
Possessing the powers of hearing and so forth,
one attains the name of a "virtuous friend" (kalyāṇamitra), just as, for example, a skilled physician;
this is explained at length.
Furthermore, there are four factors conducive to stream-entry:
first, associating with virtuous friends;
second, hearing the true Dharma.
Third is proper mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*);
fourth is practice in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*).
Such passages are found in all the sūtras.
To hear [the teaching] and yet not believe it is still superior to not hearing it at all.
Thus, the Lotus Sūtra says:
At that time, when the assembly heard Mañjuśrī say, "You shall become buddhas," although they slandered him and did not believe him,
they subsequently fell into hell;
by this causal condition, they encountered immeasurable buddhas.
Later, upon encountering the Buddha Never-Despising, they all resolved their minds on the Great Vehicle.
Within the framework of the Three Vehicles, one must first study the teachings of the Small Vehicle before one may then study the teachings of emptiness of the Great Vehicle.
This is known because there are many scriptural proofs. First,
the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra*, fascicle six, states:
Good son, if there are sentient beings who,
regarding the vehicle of the śrāvakas or the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas...
Having failed to exert effort in the correct application of diligent cultivation,
such individuals possess inferior faculties and meager diligence;
if one were to preach to them the subtle, profound, and sublime Mahāyāna True Dharma, [it would be in vain].
Both the speaker and the listener incur great transgressions;
they also act in opposition to all Buddhas. Why is this so?
If there are sentient beings who [apply themselves] to the vehicle of the śrāvakas or the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas.
Those sentient beings who have not yet undergone diligent effort,
up to and including the point of listening to and receiving the sublime Dharma of the Mahāyāna, are truly ignorant.
They consider themselves wise and intelligent,
and so forth, until:
"Such is the retribution for the transgressions of all these sentient beings."
They have all failed to first seek out and study the Mahāyāna True Dharma; instead, they have sought out and studied the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Such is their folly.
For those who hold nihilistic views, even a human body of inferior quality is difficult to obtain;
yet it is said that they shall be able to become vessels for the noble ones,
and so forth.

Such faults as these possessed by sentient beings all arise because they have not first studied the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas before entering the Mahāyāna. Second, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states:
I have not yet planted roots of goodness;
my obstacles have not yet been purified;
and my mental continuum has not yet been perfected.
Having not yet extensively cultivated resolute conviction,
and having not yet accumulated the two kinds of provisions— merit and wisdom—
they teach all phenomena based on the inherent nature of saṃsāra.
Upon hearing this, they partially comprehend impermanence, lack of constancy, and so forth, which causes them to plant roots of merit and the like;

this refers to the first period of the Hīnayāna teachings. As for those who have already planted roots of merit, up to those who have already accumulated the provisions of merit and wisdom, and so forth.
Furthermore, based on the three kinds of lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), it is taught that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature.

Based on the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*) and so forth, it is taught that all phenomena are without arising, ceasing, and so on. This refers to the Mahāyāna teachings of the second period. Furthermore, the subsequent text states:
If there are sentient beings who have already accumulated superior roots of goodness, up to superior provisions of both merit and wisdom,
and who hear my well-expounded teachings on such things as non-arising and non-ceasing, [they will attain realization].
Believing this to be the Buddha’s teaching and knowing well what to adopt and what to reject,
one will be able to swiftly realize unsurpassed bodhi.
If one cultivates these five matters even to a minor degree,
and upon hearing this teaching of mine, believes it to be the word of the Buddha,
they shall attain immeasurable merit.
One gives rise to one's own dogmatic attachment to views (*svadṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), namely:
that all phenomena are without arising and without cessation, originally quiescent, and by nature in *nirvāṇa*.
Because one gives rise to this dogmatic attachment to one's own views, [it is so called].
They will fall away from immeasurable wisdom.
If one does not cultivate these five matters upon hearing this teaching of mine, they will give rise to great karmic obstructions, slandering it with disbelief. According to the text of this sutra:
By hearing the teachings, one practices five matters;
by possessing these five matters, one is able to have faith in the Mahāyāna.
If one does not practice these five matters, one slanders and lacks faith.
Therefore, it is known that one must certainly first study the Hīnayāna and subsequently study the Mahāyāna.
For this reason, when the Buddhas appear in the world, they first teach the Hīnayāna and later teach the Mahāyāna.
As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 465, Chapter on Learning: [The text continues with the citation from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.]
"Subhūti,
if one does not study the Dharma of the śrāvakas and the Dharma of the pratyekabuddhas universally,
one will ultimately be unable to attain the bodhisattva path of vision. The *Catuḥpariṣat-sūtra* states:
It is like a householder who has an only son;
being young and immature, the child is not yet capable of receiving instruction in even the half-syllables.
Later, as they gradually grew up, they were taught the *mañjuṣā* (the full letters). The *Pañcabodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states:
"Regarding those bodhisattvas who receive and study the bodhisattva precepts, if they study the small [vehicle] and do not study the great [vehicle], [they are deficient]."
This constitutes an offense that is non-defiled.
To study the Mahāyāna while not studying the Hīnayāna constitutes an offense that is also defiled. [Sources: *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, etc.]
They all say:
"Because sentient beings are unable to hear the Mahāyāna,
it would be better not to speak at all and instead enter parinirvāṇa."
Because the Brahma King requested that he first preach the Hīnayāna,
according to these passages,
it is known.
Those who wish to study the Great Dharma must first study the teachings of the Hīnayāna. Now, upon careful examination,
there are briefly four reasons why the sūtras state that one should first study the Hīnayāna and subsequently study the Mahāyāna.
Because the One Great Vehicle is profound, subtle, and difficult to believe, one immediately gives rise to slander.
As the Lotus Sūtra says:
"If one were to praise only the Buddha Vehicle..."
Sentient beings are submerged in suffering;
because they slander the Dharma and lack faith,
they fall into the three evil realms.
Second, because it gives rise to the view of annihilationism.
The *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra* states:
"If sentient beings [hold such views] regarding the Śrāvaka Vehicle or the Pratyekabuddha Dharma Vehicle..."
Without having undergone diligent effort in formal study,
their faculties remain unripened and inferior;
with only slight diligence, they nevertheless listen to and receive the subtle, profound, and most deep Mahāyāna True Dharma.
Such sentient beings are truly deluded;
claiming themselves to be wise, they fall into the extreme of annihilationism,
succumb to deranged conceptions, and cling to the doctrine of causelessness.
Third, they do not study the Hīnayāna but study only the Mahāyāna;
yet those who claim to be students of the Mahāyāna [do not understand] either the persons or the dharmas of the Śrāvaka-yāna.
To disparage and slander [the Dharma] invites the retribution of great suffering.
Thus, the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra* states:
"Or one may merely hear or receive the teachings of the Unsurpassed Vehicle."
They then slander, revile, obstruct, and conceal the Śrāvaka vehicle and the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, which are collectively protected and upheld by all the Buddhas.
They do not allow it to circulate widely;
seeking fame and profit, they utter such words as:
"I am a follower of the Mahāyāna; I belong to the Mahāyāna faction."
They take pleasure only in hearing, studying, receiving, and upholding the Mahāyāna,
and do not take pleasure in the vehicles of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas;
nor do they associate with those who train in the two vehicles.
In this way, those who falsely claim to belong to the Mahāyāna,
by the power of their own ignorance and arrogance,
and so forth...
Those who practice the methods of the two vehicles will slander and insult them, depriving them of their majestic power. Furthermore, it is said:
"If one disparages even a single verse or a single category among the three vehicles..."
One should not associate with them,
nor engage in friendship, nor dwell together,
nor undertake activities in concert with them.
If there are those who associate with them,
or with whom they travel and socialize,
or who dwell together with them.
Or they may engage in the same activities;
together they will certainly fall into the Avīci Hell,
and so forth.
They undergo great suffering and affliction with no foreseeable end.
Why is this? Good son, in the past, when I was practicing the bodhisattva path...
When diligently striving to realize unsurpassed wisdom,
one may seek or request even a single verse of the Śrāvaka vehicle.
...and so forth,
even to the point of relinquishing one's own body, hands, feet,
flesh, blood, skin, and bones.
The same applies to the remaining two [offerings]: the head, eyes, marrow, and brain.

Fourth, if one has not previously studied the teachings and cultivated the roots of goodness through diligent practice, one will encounter many obstacles and difficulties and will be unable to believe and understand. Question:
If that is so, for what reason do many Mahāyāna sūtras disparage the training in the Hīnayāna and praise the training in the Mahāyāna as the ultimate practice?
The *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra-vivaraṇa* itself explains:
"Therefore, those of all three vehicles should practice and study;
they must not be arrogant or falsely claim to belong to the Mahāyāna while slandering the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas."
I have previously spoken these words only for those who are firm practitioners and vessels for the Mahāyāna,
saying that only by practicing the Mahāyāna can one attain the ultimate goal.
Therefore, the teachings of the past and the present do not contradict one another;

the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* and other such texts should all be interpreted in accordance with this principle. If that is so, would it not be the case that there are those of the Mahāyāna lineage who do not require the accumulation of practice?
One can only believe and understand the Mahāyāna upon hearing it.
The answer is that the lineages of the three vehicles depend on prior cultivation of roots of goodness;
there is no such thing as an inherent, natural distinction between the three vehicles by way of their original nature.
The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*, fascicle one, states:
"One is not called a bodhisattva by virtue of one's nature (*prakṛti*).
That sentient beings possess the element (*dhātu*) is what is called the mind of desire."
When the mind thus desires the causes and conditions of wholesome karma,
the arousal of the bodhicitta is called the "clan" (gotra) of a bodhisattva.
There are not merely one or two such passages.
Furthermore, there are two types of the Hīnayāna Dharma.
First is the Hīnayāna Dharma,
which refers to the teaching that explains suffering, emptiness, impermanence, dependent origination, and so forth.
Second, they give rise to the mind of the Hīnayāna;
this refers to those who, relying on its teachings,
accumulate roots of goodness through repeated practice.
Only then can one believe in the Mahāyāna;
it is not said that one first gives rise to the mind of the Two Vehicles and only afterwards studies the Mahāyāna.
One does not give rise to the mind of the two vehicles;
as for one who gives rise to the Mahāyāna mind,
although they may study the Hīnayāna, [they do not fall back].
It is not called "indeterminate";
it is called the "nature of a bodhisattva. Now, one should raise a counter-objection: if that were so, then...
If one must encounter conditions and accumulate roots of goodness before being able to believe in the Mahāyāna,
then those who could have given rise to such faith upon hearing the teaching would already have been saved by previous Buddhas.
Why is it that even to this day there are those who possess the nature of parinirvāṇa yet fall into the three evil realms?
Furthermore, the treatise states that beings in hell can achieve the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*). Regarding this, some propose the following explanation:
If there exists the natural lineage for nirvāṇa, as well as the faculties of the One Vehicle (ekayāna) and so forth,
then there are distinct characteristics;
that is to say, by their very nature, they spontaneously feel weary of saṃsāra.
They delight in nirvāṇa,
their afflictions are slight and few,
and they do not engage in coarse or evil acts such as severing the roots of virtue.
This extensively refutes the characteristic of being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
Is this statement correct or incorrect?
Answer: This statement is incorrect.
Question: On what basis is this known?
Answer: Because it contradicts both reason and scripture.
Regarding the contradiction with reason:
Since beginningless time, they have been able to feel weary of saṃsāra and take delight in nirvāṇa;
their afflictions are slight and they do not engage in coarse or evil conduct,
gradually cultivating and refining themselves through practice.
Furthermore, they must have already entered parinirvāṇa in the realm [of reality] beforehand,
because time has no beginning;
this is stated in the *Kāraṇaprajñapti-śāstra*.
Those who have exclusively practiced evil and completely severed their roots of goodness lack the causal conditions for virtue;
this is what is meant by being "without nature at the limit of time.
Yet, even now, such persons still exist.
Furthermore, if one possesses an innate nature that inherently bears the marks of the seals [of liberation],
yet universally severs the roots of goodness and exclusively practices evil,
this is the characteristic of one who lacks the spiritual lineage (*agotra*).
By what distinction can one know them to be bodhisattvas or followers of the One Vehicle? As for those who claim that [the text] contradicts the scriptures,
there are the *Śīlasamvara-sūtra* and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
Regarding such statements as those in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*,
it is held that the subtle nature of a bodhisattva is obtained without cause;
this is universally accepted as the innate nature (*prakṛti*) of a bodhisattva.
Within the sūtras and śāstras, there are only two types of seal-marks (*mudrā-lakṣaṇa*):
first, the seal-mark of subtle nature;
second, the seal-mark possessing both natures.
The characteristics of the seal of subtle nature can only be known by a Buddha;
how could an ordinary person presume to explain their distinctions?
One who possesses the two kinds of nature has six seal-characteristics.
All sentient beings know that any characteristic that can be known is not the fundamental characteristic.
How could a characteristic that is knowable be the characteristic of the fundamental nature?
Furthermore, the *Ratnavyūha-sūtra* states that Prince Sudhana and others fell away from and severed their roots of goodness prior to the sixth stage (*bhūmi*).
They fall into the Avīci Hell and commit every kind of evil;
by what signs can one recognize that such individuals are bodhisattvas?

Furthermore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and other treatises all state that the seeds which take *tathatā* (suchness) as their object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) constitute the fifty-second [category].
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says: "All things possess *tathatā* as their object-condition; because they all possess it, they are distinguished into categories based on their obstructions."
Since the causes are equal,
how can their characteristics differ?
Therefore, we know.
Regarding persons, it is said that existence and non-existence of characteristics differ;
they are certainly not inherent natures.
If one were to say that, by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), there is no intrinsic nature yet characteristics can be known, [it would be untenable].
What textual evidence is there to exclude the Śrāvaka-bhūmi?
Those who are able to have faith in the Mahāyāna teachings at the present time are all those who have planted roots of merit in previous lives.
Therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā states:
"If one gives rise to even a single thought of pure faith in this sutra,
it should be known that this person has planted various roots of goodness not under one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas alone."
They have already planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable tens of millions of Buddhas;
this has been clarified above.
This treatise addresses those with such capacities, encompassing all five natures.
Because it is the root of all myriad practices.
Regarding the causes and conditions for the arising of the three teachings,
there are five points therein.
First, the conditions for the arising of all teachings;
second, the conditions for the arising of the teachings of the two vehicles;
third, the conditions for the arising of the teachings on emptiness and existence.
IV. The conditions for the arising of the Three Piṭaka teachings;
V. The conditions for the arising of this treatise’s teaching. Regarding I. The conditions for the arising of all teachings:
all Buddhas, while in the causal stage, made vows.
All were for the sake of liberating all sentient beings and enabling them to attain Buddhahood;
they practiced the bodhisattva path for three incalculable eons and realized great enlightenment.
This is because they do not seek the minor fruits within the realms of humans or devas for the sake of sentient beings;
rather, they seek great bodhi and practice manifold ascetic austerities.
Thus, the Lotus Sūtra says:
It is solely for the sake of the one great cause and condition that [the Buddha] appears in the world;
that is to say, by means of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, he opens, reveals, awakens, and leads all sentient beings [to enlightenment].
Furthermore, the *Prajñā-śāstra* states that the arousal of great bodhicitta consists of four mental states.
It is said to be vast, supreme, and constant, with a mind that is non-erroneous.
Regarding "vast" and "supreme":
it is the desire to cause all sentient beings to attain nirvana without remainder.
"Parinirvāṇa without remainder" (anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa) distinguishes [this teaching] from the nirvāṇa of the Hīnayāna.
The intent of all Mahāyāna sūtras is the same.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
There are three vehicles: the path of humans, the path of gods, and the Bodhisattva dharma. One should lead sentient beings toward the Mahāyāna path;
those who do not abide in the Great Path should be established within the two vehicles.
Those who do not abide in nirvana are attached to the blessings and pleasures of humans and devas,
yet they create the causes for nirvana;
the intent of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is likewise.
Based on the meaning of the scriptural and treatise passages cited above,
all bodhisattvas who practice the bodhisattva path and expound the three trainings,
the three vehicles, and the three baskets do so solely for the sake of the Buddha-vehicle. Regarding the conditions for the arising of the teachings of the [first] two vehicles:
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the primary;
second, the ancillary.
"Correct" means turning the wheel of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for those seeking the Śrāvaka vehicle, and [turning the wheel] for those seeking the Pratyekabuddha vehicle.
For those who seek the Great Vehicle, he teaches the twelve links of dependent origination; for those who seek both, he teaches the six pāramitās;
and for those of all three vehicles, he teaches the Dharma common to the three vehicles.
In various treatises, the general and specific applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are explained;

within the stage of application (*prayoga*), followers of the Śrāvaka vehicle also cultivate the contemplation of the three meanings of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), as well as the seven points of proficiency, the forty-four knowledges (*jñāna*), the seventy-seven knowledges, and so forth.
Therefore, the "Chapter on Universal Study" in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states:
"Prior to the Path of Seeing of the three vehicles, one must universally study [all teachings].
Thus, we know that this includes the Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, the Six Pāramitās, and so forth.
This is taught generally for the sake of the three vehicles. Regarding the conditions for the arising of the teaching on the existence of the three emptinesses:
the teaching on existence is spoken for those who have not yet planted roots of goodness.
The obscurations have not been purified;
the mental continuum has not been perfected;
and resolute conviction has not been extensively cultivated.
Having not yet accumulated the provisions of merit and wisdom, they teach that all phenomena possess an intrinsic nature and undergo arising and ceasing; such teachings are unstable and the like.
[They] plant roots of goodness.
...up to the point of causing them to accumulate the two kinds of provisions, namely merit and wisdom.
If they have already planted roots of goodness...
...up to:
"For one who has already accumulated the two kinds of provisions,
namely merit and wisdom," the Buddha further relies upon the three natures of non-essence (*niḥsvabhāva*).
It is taught that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature;
namely, the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of characteristics and the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of arising.
The ultimate lack of intrinsic nature,
which is based upon the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of characteristics.
This is the ultimate lack of intrinsic nature.
It is taught that all things are without arising and without cessation,
primordially quiescent, and by nature in a state of nirvāṇa;
furthermore, it is for the sake of those who have set out upon the Śrāvaka Vehicle.
The turning of the wheel of the Four Noble Truths is the teaching with formal instruction for the sake of the śrāvakas;
it is solely for those who have set out to cultivate the Mahāyāna.
To say that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, without arising or ceasing,
primordially quiescent, and by nature in nirvāṇa—
this is the teaching of emptiness expounded solely for those who have set out upon the Mahāyāna.
This is stated according to their manifest characteristics;
in reality, however, it is taught that existence applies universally to all three vehicles,
and the teaching of emptiness likewise applies universally to all three vehicles.

Those of fixed nature in the three vehicles who hear the Prajñāpāramitā all realize the untainted stage (*anāsrava-bhūmi*) of their respective vehicles. Fourth, regarding the conditions for the arising of the Tripiṭaka teachings:
it is said that the Sūtra Piṭaka arises from the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the [ten] powers.
First, for the sake of enabling sentient beings to attain the path of training in the superior mind;
second, for the sake of providing various diverse teachings for sentient beings;
third, for the sake of causing all sentient beings to plant roots of goodness.
Fourth, for the sake of causing those who have not yet entered the True Dharma to enter it, the Vinaya Piṭaka is taught as a natural outflow of compassion.
First, it is for the sake of providing sentient beings with the path of the treatise on the training in higher ethics.
Second, it is for the sake of teaching the various rules of training (śikṣāpada) to sentient beings.
Third, it is for the sake of causing those who have already planted roots of virtue to bring their mental continuums to fulfillment.
Fourth, regarding "causing entry into the True Dharma":
it is for the purpose of causing [beings] to receive and uphold the training rules (*śikṣāpada*). The Abhidharma Piṭaka is taught as the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of fearlessness;
first, because it is a treatise on the path based on the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*).
Second, because it discriminates the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena;
third, for the sake of those who have already achieved [realization],
so that they may attain correct liberation.

Fourth, because one has already undertaken the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) and has realized the true nature (*tattvalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena. Question: Within the *Sūtras* there are the *Vinaya* and so forth;
within the *Vinaya* there are the *Abhidharma* and so forth.
The Abhidharma contains the Sūtras and so forth;
thus, there would be no distinction between the three piṭakas.

Answer: According to one explanation in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, names are established based on what is predominant. Although within a single division of this Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, all three piṭakas may be explained concurrently.
However, when it is said that the names of the Piṭakas are established based on their predominant content,
these three names for the Tripiṭaka are established according to what they clarify;
this refers to the fact that the three Piṭakas do not constitute a complete classification [of all teachings].
Based on the meaning clarified therein, the distinctions of the Three Piṭakas are established according to those very texts. Question:
Why is it that the disciples composed only the Abhidharma, and did not compose the Sūtra Piṭaka and the Vinaya Piṭaka?
Answer: The sequence is revealed by the Sūtra Piṭaka;
that is, one should seek the sequence within the sūtras.
Why does the Blessed One teach this chapter immediately after that chapter, and so forth? This sequence follows what is appropriate for the occasion, as the Buddha is the Teacher.
When the Buddha was in the world, those who spoke thus by virtue of the Buddha’s supernatural power were likewise entitled to have their words called "sūtras.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, his disciples may not compose sūtras on their own. The Vinaya Piṭaka is that which is revealed through its origins (nidāna).
This means that within the Vinaya, one should seek the origin story (*nidāna*).

The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 9, states:
