it is precisely within those objects such as flavors that [this occurs].
The lack of capacity for wisdom regarding liberation resulting from repeated practice is called non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*). This,
together with the co-emergent mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), is collectively termed "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*).
This principle must necessarily be so. Furthermore, it is said: "Or, when sentient beings are in a state of possessing afflictions, all their non-defiled minds and their continuities [are such]."
Because it has been perfumed by the intermingling of various afflictions,
there exists a constituent factor capable of conforming to the production of afflictions;
therefore, all undefiled minds and their attendants [are not so perfumed].
It arises as a distinct appearance resembling that [object],
because it occurs in succession through the power of repeated practice; thus,
even within a body free from faults, it is still said to possess habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
The Omniscient One has forever severed [these tendencies] so that they no longer function;
nevertheless, within the mental continuum— whether defiled or non-defiled— at the stage where what is to be abandoned by seeing has already been abandoned, [they remain].
There is another [type of] habitual tendency for the arising of afflictions that conforms to birth;
it is a residue of the afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*).
That which is defiled therein is called "homogeneity" (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
All [afflictions] are severed by the vajra-like path and no longer manifest.
If they do not manifest, they are termed the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of afflictions abandoned through seeing;
these too are severed by that same path.
Based on the distinctions among the faculties, there is practice and non-practice;
according to this treatise, since the nature of the category is not the habitual tendencies of the body, one knows that it is a mental factor (*caitta*). Furthermore, it says:
If, at the stage when what is to be abandoned by cultivation has already been abandoned,
there remains within the continuum of a non-defiled mind a residual propensity for the arising of afflictions.
This is the portion of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation;
it is called the "habitual tendencies of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation.
Because it is contaminated (*sāsrava*), it has already been abandoned by those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
According to the superiority or inferiority of their faculties, there is practice or non-practice;
because the Blessed One has attained mastery over the Dharma,
those [defilements] never arise for him, just as they ultimately do not arise for one who is already free from afflictions.
Therefore, the Buddha alone is called "one whose mental continuum is perfectly pure.

Precisely because of this, his conduct is free from error, and he attains the unique qualities such as the three foundations of mindfulness (*trīṇi smṛtyupasthānāni*). This should be understood according to the two previous explanations.
Their general meaning is the same,
though the reasons differ.
The previous explanation [held that it was] because of not diligently seeking wisdom.
Furthermore, when dharmas with distinct characteristics coexist,
they mutually act as causes to induce and produce habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Later, this will be explained by means of an undefiled mind.
Furthermore, through the continuous stream [of consciousness] being perfumed by the intermingling of various afflictions,
there exists a capacity for the production of the functional tendencies that give rise to afflictions.
Based on this as a cause, habitual tendencies (vāsanā) are induced.
This refers to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) not grasping the body—this is the original meaning of Master Yu.
To cite this passage as proof that [the seeds] also grasp the body as habitual tendencies is an error.
Therefore, it is known with certainty that [this ignorance] does not pertain to the body.
In the *Nyāyabindu-prakaraṇa*, within the section on distinguishing [types of ignorance], it says:

"Furthermore, if one is deluded regarding the specific (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) characteristics of an object, this is called the first characteristic of afflicted ignorance (*kliṣṭājñāna*)."
If one does not realize, as they truly are, the characteristics of all phenomena—such as their taste, potency, maturation, quality, number, measure, location, time, similarity, and difference.
This is the second characteristic of non-defiled ignorance; by analogy with this,
one should know that the two explanations in the *Nyāya* [treatise] maintain that there is only mind (*citta*).
The reason the mind is characterized by habitual tendencies (vāsanā) is that the wisdom associated with it is termed "non-defiled ignorance" (akliṣṭājñāna).
This follows from the correct reasoning established above.

Since these two texts agree with the *Mahāvibhāṣā* in taking the latencies of false knowledge as their essence, we know that they likewise agree with the *Mahāvibhāṣā* in being exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) in nature. Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
There exists an inferior, ignorant, non-obscured, and indeterminate nature that can obstruct liberation;
this is the essence of the obstacle to liberation. Furthermore, it is said:
"All the great masters unanimously declare..."
The refinement of the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) is entirely for the purpose of eliminating the power of the afflictions abandoned through seeing and meditation that have been induced [by them].
Regarding the manifestation of non-obscured, neutral ignorance (*anivṛtāvyākṛtājñāna*), one should understand it by analogy with the two preceding passages.
It is established that the indeterminate [factors] are mental concomitants (*caitta*).
If they also pertain to the wholesome or to the body, they are likewise included.
What scriptural evidence is there for this?
Furthermore, it contradicts reason:
generally speaking, what is called "false wisdom" cannot be termed "right wisdom."
That which is non-cognition cannot be called cognition.
Wisdom that is well-associated is termed right knowledge;
how, then, could it be termed wrong knowledge?
And is it called "ignorance"?
Furthermore, just as a non-fragrant object that has been perfumed by the smelling of fragrance possesses the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) for smelling fragrance,
a fragrant object does not do so.
Therefore, it is known that the indeterminate (avyākṛta) receives perfuming, whereas the wholesome and unwholesome do not.
Based on the principles and teachings above, the meaning is extremely clear: it must certainly be the indeterminate.
Since there is neither principle nor teaching [to the contrary], [it is established].
"How can it be that the entire body is permeated by goodness? Regarding the second explanation, which addresses external objections:
someone raises the objection, "If only the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) is not permeated by goodness, [then how can this be so?]"
If an Arhat in the formless realm were to manifest a wholesome mind, he should be called a Buddha;
at that time, he would not be failing to accomplish non-defiled ignorance. To this, it is replied:
According to the intent of this objection, one cannot grasp the intended meaning [of the sūtra]:
that there is a difference between the Buddha and the two vehicles regarding non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*).
The discussion merely concerns arising and non-arising to explain their distinct characteristics;
the wording is identical throughout,
and there is not a single passage that speaks of a distinction between establishment and non-establishment.
When an Arhat of the formless realm brings forth a wholesome mind,
although they do not achieve the non-defiled ignorance that is identical to that of a Buddha,
they are nonetheless equal to a Buddha in this regard.
However, the Buddha does not arise;
because the Arhat arises, he is not called a Buddha.
Since this objection is not a valid objection, [the original position stands].
Furthermore, where there is no pattern, there is no pattern;
where principle is complete, there is no principle.
Thus we know that non-defilement by ignorance is invariably and exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Third, regarding the passage concerning the universal application to delusion:
The *Wangtong lun* (Treatise on the Pervasion of Delusion) states:
"The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* explains that the knowledge of the characteristics of wrong conduct is termed 'wrong' because it is not true knowledge;
therefore, it is described as indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)."
In the *Nyāya*, it is stated to be indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) because it presents the nature of the obstacles to liberation and the obstacles to the faculties;
however, since it now generally presents the nature of all non-defiled ignorance, it also extends to the category of the wholesome (*kuśala*). Now, let us examine this in detail.
This interpretation is entirely devoid of logical coherence.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* merely explains that the cognition of the characteristics of wrong conduct is called "wrong" because it is not known as it truly is;
therefore, it is said to be "indeterminate."
Now, when it is said that all non-defiled ignorance is explained,
does this also include those who know things as they truly are? If one knows things as they truly are, [how could they be ignorant?]
This is therefore not ignorance.
Thus, the *Nyāya* explains the distinction, saying:
"If one cannot perceive [the object] as it truly is—such as its taste, ripeness, potency, and so forth—"
This is the characteristic of non-defiled ignorance;
by this standard, how could one grasp it as "knowing things as they truly are"? Furthermore, the *Wangtong lun* states:
"There are two kinds of ignorance."
First, the power of an obstacle to what is wholesome is weak;
second, the power of an obstacle to the indeterminate is superior.
(*Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*)
The *Nyāya* (Correct Principle) speaks according to what is predominant,
and thus says it is "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*). Here, however,
we say it is "comprehensive of the wholesome" (*kuśala*).
Furthermore, based on the views of those of inferior intelligence, an objection is raised:
"The *Nyāyānusāra* states that the sense faculties (*indriya*) and obstructions (*āvaraṇa*) may be indeterminate (*avyākṛta*);
however, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* does not clarify the nature of the sense faculties and obstructions."
Why is it not explained as being inferior?
Furthermore, regarding the interpretation of the meaning of the dharma,
although both versions have textual authority, one should follow that which is more extensive in principle.
Since there is neither scriptural authority nor logical reasoning to support the claim that a single passage definitively explains another passage as being of a virtuous nature,
how can you insist upon such a virtuous nature?
Section on the Indeterminate: Fourth, refuting divergent views.
According to the *Nyāyānusāra* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, non-afflicted ignorance has wisdom alone as its essential nature.
The text is extremely clear.
How can anyone maintain that it applies to other dharmas?
If such an interpretation exists, it is unworthy of being recorded in the text.
How can you erroneously present the explanations of the eleven masters while collectively contradicting the treatise? The first master says:
"Non-afflicted ignorance, until one has attained Buddhahood, is the dull, resultant consciousness (*vipāka-citta*)."
Regarding its essential nature as mental factors (*caitta*), the second master says that until one attains Buddhahood,
it has as its nature the dull fourfold neutral minds and their associated mental factors. The third master, the Western teacher Guṇaprabha, says:
The first [master] says that its essence consists of the dull, indeterminate minds and mental factors belonging to the period prior to attaining Buddhahood.
The fourth master says that its essence consists of the dull *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneity of the group) belonging to the period prior to attaining Buddhahood.

Based on this homogeneous character (sabhāgatā), the wisdom and other faculties that arise therein do not clearly perceive their objects. The above four masters—if their accounts are not misstated—are [of the view that this is] indeterminate (avyākṛta).
This explains that there is a slight degree of cognition.
Thus, it should be understood according to the sūtras and śāstras;
for in the *Nyāyānusāra* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, it is clearly stated that its essential nature is exclusively non-defined wisdom (*avyākṛta-prajñā*).
For what reason, then, do the first three masters claim that it comprises both mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*)?
Regarding the fourth master’s position on whether [ignorance] takes the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) as its object:
one should say that although the first three differ in their explanations regarding whether ignorance is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and its scope,
they all take wisdom (*prajñā*) as their essential nature.
The fourth [master] should state that its essence consists of inferior wisdom produced by a dull homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
The fifth master holds that its essence is lack of self-mastery (*asvatantrya*);
he cites the *Nyāyabindu* (Treatise on Logic) 7.0 to provide proof for this master’s interpretation as being the essence of the obstacle to liberation (*mokṣāvaraṇa*). The sixth master says:
The seventh teacher says that its essence consists in not seeking diligently and so forth.
Both of these [positions] also cite the *Nyāyānusāra* as evidence, asserting that it brings about the emergence from the obstacles to liberation.
According to the masters who follow the *Nyāyānusāra*, there are four different explanations regarding the nature of the obstacle to liberation (*vimokṣāvaraṇa*).
One master asserts that its nature consists of neutral (*avyākṛta*) and inferior wisdom (*hīnaprajñā*);
this [view] takes non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*) as its essence.
The *Nyāyānusāra* explains this in detail as the correct meaning:
the latter three [obstructions] all do not take non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*) as their essence.
The *Nyāyānusāra* extensively refutes these three masters because their definitions of the essence of the obstacle to liberation differ;
it is not that they disagree regarding the essential nature of non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*).
The *Nyāyānusāra* (Seventy Verses on Right Reasoning) states that all [opposing views] are refuted by saying "it is not admitted," which clearly indicates this point.
It does not say that "not admitted" refers to non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*).
Thus, one should understand that these three masters differ in their explanations regarding what constitutes an obstruction (*āvaraṇa*).
To claim that this is "non-defiled ignorance" (akliṣṭājñāna) is a grave error,
as it contradicts the definition of the substance of the teaching.
Some say it is sound;
others say it is names and phrases.
If it were to further produce the substance of sound, how could it be called "sound"? Or if names and phrases were taken as its substance, [how could it be so?]
Regarding the latter four masters' explanations, these are refutations established by the treatise itself;
as they are not accepted by our own school, they will not be recounted in detail. Fifth, the description of the universality or particularity of the essence.
Its essence consists of non-defiled ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*), which is unobscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), and it is characterized by inferior wisdom (*hīnaprajñā*).
It pervades all four types of indeterminate states.
One should not doubt that its nature is that of a mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
Thus it is known that the subtle wisdom associated with the latencies of deportment and craftsmanship is termed non-defiled ignorance. By attaining this,
the followers of the two vehicles equally fulfill their requirements and transcend the pitfall.
Kāśyapa’s dancing was a habituation to that deportment;
Piṅgala’s calling upon the river deity as "little maid" and so forth were likewise [habitual tendencies].
This is the habitual tendency (*vāsanā*) of craftsmanship;
therefore, it is known that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are of three types of neutral (*avyākṛta*).
Regarding those that involve transformation (*nirmāṇa*):
There are those that appear to arise as transformations of greed, anger, and so forth;
however, no scriptural authority for this has been seen.
These are all merely habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Thus, it is known that [this category] also extends to transformations (*nirmāṇa*).
Regarding the sixth pair, which distinguishes the differences, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Correct Principles) provides three interpretations. The first interpretation states:
"Now, to examine this in detail..."
The distinction between the two types of ignorance is as follows:
it is by virtue of this that the difference between delusion and wisdom is established.
This is called the characteristic of defiled ignorance.
If, by virtue of this, there are cases where wisdom does not reach what is within the scope of ignorance, this is the second characteristic. The commentary states:
"Ignorance" refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*);
"wisdom" refers to noble ones (*ārya*).
Those who have severed [ignorance] are called noble ones;
those who have not severed it are called ordinary beings.
This distinction between the deluded and the wise is established based on afflicted ignorance.
There may be an object that an arhat does not recognize, such as red salt,
while an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) proficient in the Tripiṭaka does recognize it;
this is called ignorance regarding the inferiority of knowledge with respect to an object.
Based on these differing characteristics, it cannot be said that non-afflicted ignorance (akliṣṭājñāna) pervades the supporting body (*āśraya*). The second explanation states:
"Furthermore, if [it] has already been severed..."
There is no distinction between the Buddha and those of the two vehicles;
this is the first characteristic.
If there were any severance, [it would not be so].
The Buddha and those of the two vehicles differ in that [the former] has practice while [the latter] do not;
this is the second characteristic. The commentary states:
"Defiled ignorance is severed equally by all three vehicles."
Once severed, they do not function because their intrinsic nature has been severed;
thus, they are all without distinction.
Non-afflicted ignorance is severed equally by all three vehicles.
Because the bonds of conditions have been severed,
the two vehicles may still practice it,
whereas only a Buddha does not.
Thus there is a distinction. The third explanation states:
"If one is deluded regarding the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena, this is called the first characteristic of afflicted ignorance."
If one cannot, with regard to the characteristics of all phenomena— such as their taste, potency, maturation, quality, number, measure, location, time, similarity, and difference—
perceive them as they truly are.
This is non-defiled ignorance. The commentary states:
Defiled ignorance is delusion regarding specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

Non-defiled ignorance refers to [delusion regarding] the flavor of phenomena, the taste of phenomena, or the flavor of their power such as suffering and so forth; the efficacy of phenomena such as benefit and harm; the ripening of phenomena to the stage of maturation; the qualities and functions; numbers such as one and two; magnitudes such as large and small; locations such as near and far; times such as recent and distant; and similarities and differences. This follows the third explanation.
Non-defiled ignorance is also not the supporting body. Seventh, regarding the distinctions of abandonment:
defiled ignorance has three meanings, the first of which is abandonment by way of its own nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*).
This refers to the power of the path of antidotes;
because it is called "abandonment" at the moment one relinquishes those [defilements],
the bonds of the objects of cognition are severed.
This means that with respect to the bodies of others, it is called "severing the bonds of conditions.
One severs the afflictions directed toward the bodies of others;
it is only upon reaching the ninth stage [of the path of cultivation] that this is termed "severance."
If one looks toward one's own person, there is the severance of conditions and bonds,
and the third is the severance through non-arising;
that is to say, when all afflictions reach the state of non-arising, they attain ultimate non-arising.
Just as the afflictions of the path of seeing [are abandoned] up to the stage of supreme patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*),
so too are the afflictions of the path of cultivation;
those of sharp faculties do not emerge from meditative absorption to abandon the afflictions.
At the time of the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*),
those nine grades of afflictions obtain the state of never arising again;
however, because a noble one of dull faculties may still regress, there is no "non-arising abandonment" (*anutpāda-prahāṇa*) [for them].
Bodhisattvas and those like the rhinoceros horn [pratyekabuddhas] ensure that the afflictions of both the path of vision and the path of cultivation do not arise;
this is not the case for other types of śrāvakas and the like.
Within the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*), it is also possible for the afflictions of seeing and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-kleśa*) not to arise;
however, because their characteristics are not manifest, they are not described here.
As for all other [afflictions], there is none that is not abandoned through cessation. There are two types of abandonment regarding non-defiled ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*).
First is the severance of the bond of objects.
This refers to the time when, upon severing the ninth grade of defiled ignorance in each respective stage,
one attains the severance of the bond of objects.
Second is abandonment through non-arising,
which means attaining ultimate non-arising at various respective stages.
Second is partial abandonment by the two vehicles.
Because the Buddha has completely severed [them]. Eighth, regarding the description of the stages of severance, there are two parts therein:
first, the partial severance.
Regarding the two types— complete abandonment and partial abandonment:
when, in various respective stages, [defilements] never arise again,
at that time they are said to be abandoned.
Regarding those who have completely severed the hindrances to the faculties and so forth:
when a bodhisattva reaches the diamond-like mind (*vajropamasamādhi*),
at that time they universally attain the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) of all non-afflicted ignorance.
At that time, when they are completely exhausted,
although one may attain great enlightenment from a single sitting through the five contemplations for settling the mind,
at that moment they will never again arise.
However, the attainment of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) necessarily occurs upon reaching the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*). This is just as,
for example, although conventional minds at the conclusion of direct realization (*abhisamaya*) never arise again, [they have nonetheless been ceased].
Upon reaching the conclusion of the third category of knowledge (*trividya-jñāna*), one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),
because at that time the superior conditions [for further arising] are absent.
Regarding those superior conditions, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "That is to say, their supporting body;
that supporting body is identical to that of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*)."
At the time of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), there is no possibility for [the afflictions] to arise.
When one emerges from contemplation (*vyutthāna*), the basis [upon which they would arise] has already ceased;
since the superior basis is lacking, they cannot arise. Question: Do noble beings (*ārya*) of sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*) sever the afflictions without emerging from contemplation?
The nine afflictions attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) during the stage of the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*);
non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*) should be treated in the same manner.
Consequently, it should attain non-arising (*anutpāda*) at the stage of the five mental abidings (*pañca-vastuka*).
Answer: Until one has attained Buddhahood, it is possible for [the storehouse consciousness] to serve as the basis for a certain type of non-defiled ignorance.
This type of non-defiled ignorance...
When superior conditions are lacking,
the body cannot arise;
even if one were to dwell within the thirty-three states of mind.
If a distracted mind arises, it is also possible that [the object] will not be understood,
because at that time one has not yet attained all-encompassing wisdom (sarvajñā),
and because the path is not its direct antidote.
Furthermore, for example, among the nine types of physical bases within the desire realm, each of these bodies can serve as a basis for the afflictions;
since the Path is the direct antidote to the afflictions,
this principle cannot be used as a precedent.
Furthermore, even if one were to emerge from contemplation with thirty-three moments of mind,
one's wisdom would still not equal that of a Buddha.
When emerging from meditative absorption through the thirty-two moments of mind,
wisdom is again even more inferior;
other states of mind are to be understood accordingly.
Therefore, one should know that non-afflicted ignorance arises as distinct moments of mind and is abandoned through distinct categories;
how could it be the same as the afflictions? Thus says the Treatise.
Having already praised the Blessed One up to the perfection of his qualities for the benefit of others,
the following third section describes those qualities of benefiting others;
this serves as a transitional summary.
Commentary:
"To pull sentient beings out of the mire of birth and death" is a restatement of the verse text. As for the term "sentient beings":
This is another name for *sattva*.
In the Sanskrit language, it is called *sattva*; this is translated as "sentient being" (*yǒuqíng*).
The Sanskrit name is *sattva* (pronounced with a rising tone on the final syllable);
this is translated as "sentient beings" (*zhòngshēng*). It is identical in substance to *sattva* (sentient beings), though the names differ.
Some say that if one uses the term "sentient beings," it includes both the sentient and the insentient.
Therefore, it is an error to say that [the term] refers only to sentient beings.
Thus, the Mahāyāna-saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra and the Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra [state this].
He addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One,
what is the meaning of 'sentient beings'?"
The Buddha told the Lord of Laṅkā:
"Sentient beings are a combination of various elements."
Earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness—
just as bundles of reeds stand leaning against one another,
so it is said that sentient beings [exist]. According to this scriptural passage, those who possess feeling (*sattva*) are called "sentient beings" (*sattva*).
This is to refute the notion that there exists a separate entity as the essence of a sentient being; furthermore, according to this text,
"sentient being" (sattva) and "living being" (jīva) differ in name but are identical in substance.
Sentient beings are composed of the six elements;
sentient beings are likewise.
One cannot point to any single dharma and designate it as the essence of a sentient being.
The Vijñānavādins point to the single substantial entity of the ālayavijñāna as the essence of sentient beings; it is not,
therefore, a composite of the six elements.
The treatise does not explicitly state that sentient beings are provisional and not real.
It explains the meaning of "mud" in the verse by means of the analogy of how their birth and death are like mud.
The three realms and five destinies are the abodes of birth and death.
Karma mixed with the waters of craving is like mud;
once situated therein, one sinks and is submerged.
To emerge from it is difficult;
because one descends gradually, it is called "sinking," and thus termed "immersion.
Since the ninety-five types [of heterodox views] cannot be abandoned, it is difficult to emerge.
One who dwells in the mud will inevitably sink;
one with little strength cannot emerge from it.
Because these two meanings are identical, the mud is used as a metaphor.
Treatise:
"Among them, [the Buddha] reaches out to rescue and deliver [beings]" explains his debt of gratitude and virtue.
"Beings are submerged therein, with no means of escape"—this is the realm of compassion. The World-Honored One feels pity for them.
This is great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). The hand that bestows the appropriate teachings of the True Dharma according to [the needs of beings] is skillful means and wisdom (*upāya-prajñā*).
To extract and rescue [beings] is the fulfillment of compassionate activity. As stated in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*:
Those who possess skillful wisdom and great compassion grant appropriate instructions and rescue them,
causing them to emerge [from suffering].
This means that one desires to rescue others because of compassion,
and is able to rescue them because of skillful wisdom;
this is great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Although these are designated by different names, such as "skillful wisdom" (kauśalyajñāna),
they are all subsumed under the Buddha’s outflow-tainted wisdom (sāsravajñāna) of benefit for others (arthakriyā).
It constitutes the essence of the benefactor's kindness;
it also includes the accompanying conduct,
as explained in the standard commentaries.
Treatise:
Having already praised the virtues of the Buddha, one next pays respectful homage.
What follows below is the fourth section, which describes the characteristics of this respectful homage.
This is the introduction to the treatise.
Homage is thus paid.

"Reaching the name 'Teacher of Reality' (yathārtha-śāstṛ)" introduces the verse and provides its commentary. "Bowing my head to his feet, I pay homage" explains the two characters "homage" (namas) of the verse.
"Khai" (稽) means "to reach" (zhì); "shou" (首) refers to the "head."
Placing one's own head at the Buddha's feet signifies the expression of respectful salutation;
such salutation encompasses the three modes of action (body, speech, and mind).
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:

"With my body, speech, and mind, I prostrate at the feet of the World-Honored One. Although Master Vasubandhu speaks here specifically of the body, he must necessarily include all three types of action (*trikarma*).

among the seventy-five dharmas, it takes *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through deliberation) as its essence.
For each individual atom and each individual moment of contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*),
there is a distinct analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) upon each respective phenomenon.
Therefore, various treatises state:
"The measure of analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is equal to the measure of the objects to which one is bound. First, regarding the explanation of its name:
the distinction of wholesome wisdom is termed "analysis" (pratisaṃkhyā).
That which is realized through the power of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*) is called "cessation through discernment" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);
this is a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound. Regarding the distinctions in its attainment, there are four types therein.
First, an exposition of the correct meaning;
second, an account of divergent views;
third, an exposition of [views] that contradict reason and scripture.
Fourth, explaining away external objections. First, stating the correct meaning:
one’s own afflictions, their co-existent factors, and their acquisitions.
When one attains detachment from the body through the arising of the specific counteractive path corresponding to each respective category [of defilement],
that dharma undergoes analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

At that time, it is called "attainment," because one attains cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) by means of the abandonment of its own intrinsic nature. This applies to the defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*) of another's continuum,
as well as all material form (*rūpa*).
It is untainted by the outflows of the formless realm;
it consists of all unconditioned phenomena,
because the afflictions directed toward those phenomena within one's own continuum have reached ultimate exhaustion.

At that time, the unconditioned factors (asaṃskṛta-dharma) residing upon the bound phenomena arise as acquisitions (prāpti), because the fetters (bandhana) have been severed. Question: How is this known to be so?
The answer is found in the Anuśaya-nirdeśa chapter of this treatise,
which states: "Based on this,
it should be explained from what specific source the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth is determined."

The abandonment of afflictions and so forth within one's own continuum occurs through the attainment of abandonment; likewise, there is the abandonment of afflictions and so forth within the continua of others,
as well as the abandonment of all form and non-defiled phenomena.
Because one is able to bring about the ultimate abandonment of all afflictions within one’s own continuum that take those [objects] as their objective support— according to this treatise,
it is known that:
These two types of abandonment result in the attainment of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Question:

Furthermore, according to what textual authority is it proven that the abandonment of the acquisition of afflictions (*kleśa-prāpti*) constitutes abandonment by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*), whereas the non-defiled dharmas and so forth constitute abandonment by way of the severance of objective fetters (*ālambana-bandhana-prahāṇa*)? Answer: This treatise, in its sixteenth fascicle, states: [text follows].
For what reason can only the final path abandon the contaminated wholesome dharmas of the various stages, and not any other?
Because wholesome dharmas are not abandoned by their own nature;
once abandoned, they may still manifest.
However, it is when the afflictions that take them as objects are exhausted [that they are truly severed].
Only then can it be said that those wholesome dharmas have been severed,
because at that time the wholesome dharmas attain dissociation from their fetters. Consequently,
this continues until the afflictions that take them as objects [are also eliminated].
One category remains; thus,
the sense of abandonment is not established,
because at that time the wholesome dharmas have not yet been disjoined from their fetters.
According to the aforementioned treatise,
it is known that when [defilements] have been severed and no longer function, this is called "severance by intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*).
That which is abandoned once [the afflictions] have been severed is the object of abandonment.
Furthermore, in the sixth chapter of the *Nyāyānusāra*,
the great masters of the Abhidharma state:
Based on what is taught in the sūtras, two kinds of abandonment are established:
first, abandonment by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*);
second, abandonment by object (*ālambana-prahāṇa*). If a dharma is a fetter (*saṃyojana*), as well as having a single fruit (*eka-phala*) and so forth.
When the antidote arises,
its abandonment is termed "abandonment by way of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*). Because of that abandonment,
one attains dissociation (*visamyoga*) from the objective basis (*ālambana-vastu*).
It is not necessary that non-attainment within this [state] be termed the "severance of the object-condition" (*ālambana-prahāṇa*).
Herein, all contaminated form (*rūpa*) and all uncontaminated yet contaminated formless states (*arūpya*) are included.

Furthermore, those various acquisitions (prāpti) and dharmas such as arising (jāti) are bound by fetters (saṃyojana) that are abandoned through seeing (darśana-heya) and abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
When these various fetters (*saṃyojana*) are abandoned gradually, the attainment of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*) arises with respect to each distinct category of them.

Those fetters, as well as their single fruit (*eka-phala*), are all termed "already abandoned. The above explains abandonment by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*). Regarding the term "single fruit": [it refers to the fact that] for each category of fetter, there is a single fruit.
"Connected with the fetters, co-existent, and so forth.
The term "and so forth" includes acquisition (*prāpti*).

This refers to the acquisitions of disconnection (*visamyoga-prāpti*) regarding those tainted material phenomena (*rūpa*), as well as those tainted non-material phenomena (*arūpa*) that are not afflicted (*akliṣṭa*), along with their respective acquisitions, and the factors such as arising (*jāti*) and so on.
At that time, [the affliction] has not yet arisen;
therefore, it is not yet called "abandoned.
Because those dharmas merely follow that final [moment], the abandonment of the object (ālambana-prahāṇa) is explained according to the aforementioned treatise.
One's own afflictions,
as well as the co-existent dharmas and the acquisitions (prāpti) of these two types of dharmas,
are abandoned by means of their respective categories through the path of counteraction (pratipakṣa-mārga).
At the moment of attaining relinquishment (*prahāṇa*), one attains analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This is not because analytical cessation is attained through the severance of the afflictions that take [the object] as their cognitive support (*ālambana*).
Second, regarding the presentation of divergent views, there are two parts within this.
The aforementioned masters, such as the Great Dharma Master Tai and others, explain: "However,
since suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) are universally the same bond,
when one cuts off the ten [factors] below suffering, it is at that time [that they are severed]."
Although one is still bound by the pervasive underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the lower [realm] within the category of origination (*samudaya*) and has not yet severed them,
it is said that one attains dissociation (*visamyoga*) from the underlying tendencies of the lower [realm] within the category of suffering (*duḥkha*),
because the underlying tendencies of their own [respective] seeds are proximate.
When one is separated from the bondage of one's own seed,
that which is bound attains liberation;
it is like a person being freed from the shackles and fetters upon their own body.
It is said that a person attains liberation by distancing themselves from other types [of fetters].
Although they have not yet left [the prison], they are liberated;
just as a person within a prison, though they have not yet exited the prison gate, is already free from the shackles and chains upon their body within the prison.
It is called "liberated" because, within the gateway of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the nine grades of fetters (*saṃyojana*) of each category are likewise [abandoned].
When the first grade is severed,
one is said to have attained liberation through the proximate dissociation from that very category.
Although the eighth category of remote fetters has not yet been abandoned, it is said that one attains the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) upon abandoning the first category of defiled [fetters].
The remaining eight categories may be understood by analogy with this explanation. This applies exclusively to defiled form and the other non-defiled five aggregates.
When the ninth grade of the fetters is severed,
that which was bound is then said to be liberated. (1) The Tripitaka Master of the Tang Dynasty revised the explanations of the various masters of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, stating:
Question: If one attains disjunction through the realization of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),
as when the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has already arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen,
[what happens to] those [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of suffering?
If one is still bound by the pervasive afflictions (*sarvatraga-kleśa*) associated with the lower realm, how can one realize cessation?

Furthermore, regarding the nine grades of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), if one has abandoned even a single grade up to the eighth grade, how can one realize cessation while still being bound by the subsequent grades? The explanation states: Although one attains the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) through liberation from that which binds and that which is bound once [the afflictions] have been severed, [the realization of cessation is not complete until all bonds are removed].
However, the afflictions that act as bonds vary in strength— some being strong and others weak.
One type is the bond of association (*samprayoga-bandhana*),
which refers to the afflictions binding the primary mind (*citta*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) at the same moment.
Second is the bondage of the object (ālambana-bandhana),
which means that the objects of the afflictions possess a poisonous power that binds these objects,
rendering them incapable of being mastered.
Within the context of the fetters of conditions, there are subsequently four types:
first, those of the same category and the same class;
second, those of the same category but different classes.
Third, the same category within a different school;
fourth, a different category within a different school. Together with the preceding associated factors, there are five fetters in total.
Among these five fetters, one abandons the strongest and realizes their cessation through direct realization.
The weak are not proofs; as for what is called "strong" and "weak":
first, those bound by association have the strongest force;
second, those bound by the same category and the same type have the next strongest force.
Third, the bondage of the same category and different aspect has the next strongest power.
Fourth, the bondage of a different category and the same aspect has a slightly weaker power.
Fifth, the bondage of a different category and a different aspect has the weakest power. Among these five types of bondage, the first three are strong.
The latter two are weak.
If one abandons the former three, one realizes their respective analytical cessations (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);
as for the latter two types, their power to bind is subtle.

It is not by means of abandoning them that one realizes cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). For example, regarding the phenomena (*dharma*) abandoned through the vision of suffering, there are generally two types:
one type consists of associated phenomena (*saṃprayukta-dharma*), and the other type consists of acquisition (*prāpti*) and the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Associated dharmas possess five fetters (*bandhana*).
When they are associated with the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) excluding the characteristic of acquisition (*prāpti*), there remain four fetters.
This is the case when the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has already arisen, but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen.
The factors associated with what is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering are abandoned by means of severing the associated fetters and the fetters of the same category and the same type.
Because they are bound by being of the same category but different classes;
because the attainment of cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is attained through the power of abandonment;
and because it possesses the four characteristics (lakṣaṇas).
Because one abandons the fetters of the same category and the same type,
as well as those of the same category and a different type,
one realizes cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), for such abandonment is powerful.
When these associated factors, their acquisition, and the four characteristics arise,
although one is at that time bound by the pervasive afflictions of the lower realms— both within the same category and across different categories—
the realization of cessation is attained because those afflictions are extremely weak.
Furthermore, at that time, although one has severed the bonds of the latter four categories—
namely, those abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) that consist of both similar and dissimilar classes within different categories—
one is still unable to realize the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) of those latter four categories.
Because they have not yet been severed,
the nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) are severed as a single grade;
this is because the afflictions to be abandoned are categorized into nine grades.
Thus, one can speak of the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*).

As with those abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), it should be understood by analogy that those abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), and the path (*mārga*) each have two categories. Those abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga-prahātavya*) comprise three categories in total.
Dharmas associated with defilement constitute one category.
The acquisition (*prāpti*) and the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of dharmas associated with defilement constitute another category.
All other contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas constitute yet another category.
That is to say: defiled matter, along with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) regarding that matter and the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*);
as well as the five non-defiled aggregates (*skandha*). Of these, the first category possesses all five fetters (*bandhana*);
the latter two categories each possess four fetters, excluding the fetter of association (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*), because they are dissociated (*viprayukta*).
Therefore, when one abandons the defiled factors associated with the first category,
one realizes the unconditioned through the abandonment of the bonds of association and the bonds of the same class and category;
this is because such abandonment is powerful.
At that time, although one is bound by the remaining eight categories belonging to the same category but different classes,
because these are inferior bonds, one also realizes the unconditioned;
this is not the case during the path of seeing.

Because in the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), each of the nine grades is abandoned one by one, those of the same category (*nikāya*) and the same grade (*prakāra*) may both be said to be strong; however, those of different grades within the same category are said to be weak.

Alternatively, it may be that in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the nine grades are abandoned separately, and thus those of the same category but different grades are designated as weak. Or perhaps [it is as follows].
In the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), those belonging to the same category but different classes are also termed "weak.
This is like ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who abandon the five categories in a mixed manner;
as they abandon each preceding class, [the subsequent ones are likewise weak].
They are still bound by the afflictions of the delusions of view;
because they are weak and inferior, they also realize cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Thus it is said.
Therefore, it is known that this [defilement] is weak.
This is because, in the case of other categories, the pervasive defilements belonging to both the similar and dissimilar classes have already been abandoned;
even if those were not abandoned, one would still realize the unconditioned.
Because the fetters are inferior,
the four characteristics of the defiled acquisition of the first category arise;
when this first category is abandoned, [the characteristics of abandonment likewise arise].
By severing the bonds of the same category and the same type,
one realizes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) because of the severance of that which is powerful.
The cases of the same category and different types, as well as different categories and both same and different types, are all to be understood according to the preceding explanation.
As with the abandonment of the first category, the remaining eight categories may be understood by analogy.
Other contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) likewise consist of nine categories,
as they correspond in their respective degrees of intensity.
Regarding the explanation of similar and dissimilar classes:
when abandoning other contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*),
one abandons the fetters (*bandhana*) of the same category, the same class, and the dissimilar class.
Because the [defilements] to be abandoned are strong, one realizes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) upon their cessation.

Regarding those of other categories or the same category that have already been previously abandoned— even if they are not currently being abandoned— one still realizes analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),
because the fetters [to be abandoned] are weak.

Furthermore, regarding these other contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) which are objects of bondage, they are only said to be "abandoned" when the nine grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) that take them as objects have been completely severed;
only then is the object itself termed "abandoned. Third, the description of contradictions with reason and scripture:
The various virtuous masters have also explained this:
although they speak of "proximate bondage," "distant bondage," and "bondage," their strength and weakness differ.
There is a distinction in the manner of abandonment;
however, they all equally state that because the afflictions which take [the object] as their cognitive support are abandoned by means of the "similar category" (sabhāga) and so forth,
one attains liberation from those afflictions that take the similar category and so forth as their objects.
Just as the nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation are mutually bound by their objects,
so too, regarding the ninth grade of affliction directed toward the cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) of a higher stage,
even if the [afflictions of] the eight lower grades have been abandoned, one cannot attain dissociation from that object.
Because they do not belong to the same category or class,
and because they are remote and inferior,
when the ninth grade is abandoned, [the afflictions are likewise severed].
Because it belongs to the same category (*nikāya*) and the same class (*jāti*),
and because it is proximate and powerful,
one attains disjunction (*visamyoga*). However, that all the virtuous ones provide this same explanation is truly marvelous and accords with reason.
However, there is no textual authority for this, and it still contradicts reason. As for what contradicts reason:
for instance, regarding the nine grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) that are to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), they take one another as objects.
What distinct cause is there for [afflictions] within their own category (*sva-nikāya*) and their own grade (*sva-prakāra*)?
For that which binds its own category and its own class, it is proximate and strong.
When binding through the objects of a different class within its own category,
what distinct principle is there to call it distant or inferior?
For example, when a weak-grade affliction takes a weak-grade object as its condition,
what distinct cause makes it strong?
And when the [final] eight grades take a weak-grade object as their condition?
When the eight higher grades [of defilements] are abandoned, one does not yet realize the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
it is only when the lower grades are abandoned that one first attains analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
If it is argued that the power [of abandonment] is equal to that which is bound [to the realm], [it is not so].
One must not say that it is "strong" because it is of an inferior grade;
for if one says its power overcomes what it is bound to, it cannot be called a "similar instance" (sapakṣa),
since power that overcomes an inferior grade is itself not of an inferior grade.
How can it be the same as the lower grade?
Therefore, it is said that it has the power to overcome the upper eight grades.
Furthermore, when the lower-grade afflictions encounter two grades [of objects] simultaneously, [it is likewise].
Is it as strong as its own class,
or as weak as a different class?
It cannot be both strong and weak within a single class.
Furthermore, when these afflictions bind themselves and other categories [of phenomena],
how could there be a distinction such that binding one's own category is strong while binding another category is weak? As for the claim that this contradicts the scriptures:
The *Nyāyānusāra*, fascicle six, states:
"Because the great masters of the Abhidharma establish two kinds of abandonment based on what is taught in the sūtras. According to this treatise, [the two kinds of abandonment are as follows].
The intention of all masters is the same: first, abandonment by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*),
which means that it is designated as "abandoned" at the moment one relinquishes [the possession] and acquires [its non-possession].
By this, one realizes the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
There are two ways in which the objects of cognition are severed:
by severing the final category of afflictions, one realizes analytical cessation.

Now, as for the established position that one attains the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) through the abandonment of the same category and the same class, as well as through the abandonment of association—
this is not abandonment by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
It is not because it is attained at the time of relinquishing [the defilements], for one attains cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);
nor is it because the object of cognition is severed,
for one realizes cessation through deliberation by means of the final category [of the path].

On what scriptural authority is this single abandonment established, while contradicting the two abandonments established by the great masters of the Abhidharma? This is the fourth point, which addresses external objections.
An objection is raised:

If it is said that when defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*) are severed and abandoned, this is called "severance by intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*) and not "severance by object" (*ālambana-prahāṇa*), [then...]
For what reason do all the treatises state that the measure of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is likewise according to the measure of the things to which it is bound?
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 31, states:
"All contaminated phenomena (sāsrava-dharma) have existed since beginningless time."
Bound by the afflictions (*kleśa*), one does not attain liberation.
If the afflictions are severed, because of that dissociation (*visaṃyoga*), one attains liberation;
just as when a person who has been bound attains release, people call that person "liberated."
This does not refer to ropes and the like;
since one attains liberation from that which binds, one also attains liberation from external objects. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other texts state:
One should know that the various afflictions can be severed by means of their objects (*ālambana*).
According to the aforementioned treatise, it is known that the various afflictions are severed through their objects;
however, this is not the same as the case of non-defiled [neutral] states.
Therefore, it is known that when the similar class (*sabhāga*) is severed, one realizes cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
The commentary states: These cited passages do not constitute definitive proof, as they are not explicit.
Who could believe such unintelligible phrasing and,
in opposition to the great masters of the Abhidharma,
establish two types of abandonment based on what is taught in the Sūtras?
A close examination of these three passages reveals that each possesses a specific intent.
For instance, regarding the citation: "Just as the number of conditioned phenomena to which one is bound is so, so too is it for the unconditioned.
This clarifies that the enumeration of analytical cessations (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) does not clarify their abandonment or realization.
This is because the Vaibhāṣika masters of differing views maintain that the unconditioned state of cessation by analysis (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is equal in measure to the objects it binds;
whereas the Dharmasāstrin masters assert it is equal in measure to the objects bound.
Furthermore, this statement was made because the Saṃmitīya school posits only a single unconditioned phenomenon.
Defiled phenomena that are not [inherently] luminous are abandoned through their objects of perception.
All contaminated phenomena have existed since beginningless time;
even as when a person who has been bound attains liberation, they are called "liberated."
Regarding the phrase "it is not said that [this applies to] the rope and so forth":
this refers to the position of certain teachers who maintain that liberation is attained with respect to the fettering agent,
rather than being attained with respect to the external phenomena that constitute the bound object.
Therefore, this statement was made.
It is not that the existence of the abandonment of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is denied by making this statement.
One should understand that it is from the object of perception (ālambana) that the various afflictions can be brought to cessation.

This is stated in accordance with the [Abhidharma] treatises; it is not intended to deny the cessation of intrinsic nature (svabhāva-prahāṇa). Regarding the similarities and differences among the four treatises:

since unconditioned analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-asamskṛta) corresponds to the number of objects to which one is bound, it is known that there is only a single analytical cessation for each individual dharma.
Furthermore, all those beyond training (aśaikṣa) realize the cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) regarding all contaminated phenomena (sāsrava-dharma).
Thus, it is known that this cessation through deliberation is necessarily realized in common [by all]. As the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), which accords with the sūtras, states:
Question: If that is so, why is nirvāṇa called an uncommon dharma?
Answer: Although the essence of nirvāṇa is common, [it is called uncommon because it is not shared by those who have not attained it].
However, it is designated as "unshared" (*āveṇika*) because the acquisition of disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*) arises individually within the personal continuum of each sentient being.
Furthermore, this is supported by a scriptural citation:
The liberation of the Tathāgata is no different from that of other Arhats;
this is said with reference to the cessation realized. Regarding the five differences in abandonment, one should now provide a formal analysis based on the types of abandonment.
There are three kinds of dharmas:
first, those dharmas obtained by one's own person;
second, those dharmas obtained by other persons.
Three are not dharmas obtained by either of the two.
First, regarding the seventy-five dharmas distinguished as those obtained by oneself:
There are those that are abandoned by [the abandonment of] their own intrinsic nature, but not by [the abandonment of] their objects;
these are the universal defilements (kleśa-mahābhūmika) and the universal unwholesome factors (akuśala-mahābhūmika).
Regarding the minor defilement ground (*parītta-kleśa-bhūmi*) and the indeterminate (*aniyata*) factors—

namely, greed, hatred, pride, and doubt— among these, those that are abandoned by means of an object (*ālambana-prahāṇa*) rather than by means of their own nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*) are the ten material factors in their entirety.
A portion of the non-informative (avijñapti), excluding that which is untainted (anāsrava);
a portion of the great wholesome mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharma);

and, among the dissociated (viprayukta) factors, all nine dissociated factors with the exception of four characteristics (lakṣaṇa) and a portion of acquisition (prāpti)—these are both abandoned by way of their intrinsic nature (svabhāva-prahāṇa) and abandoned by way of their object (ālambana-prahāṇa).
This refers to the mind-king (citta-rāja),
a portion of the ten universal mental factors (mahābhūmika) including vitarka and vicāra,
and the entirety of kaukṛtya and middha.
Regarding the four characteristics and the acquisition of a portion of the contaminated (*sāsrava*):
these are associated with, co-existent with, and acquired through the abandonment of their own nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*).
It is not that those [factors] associated with it, co-existent with it, or its acquisition (*prāpti*) are what are abandoned by the object-condition (*ālambana-prahāṇa*).
Regarding the "neither" category:

among the seventy-five dharmas, those which are untainted (*anāsrava*) are all neither of the two types of abandonment. If one were to pose questions and provide answers by referring generally to other persons' bodies:

However, all that is abandoned by way of its own nature (*svabhāva-prahīṇa*) is also abandoned by way of its object (*ālambana-prahīṇa*), because it is abandoned by others through the same single fruit of its own fetters (*sva-saṃyojana-eka-phala*).
In total, there are three propositions: excluding that which is abandoned by its own nature but not abandoned by its object.
Regarding dharmas obtained by another’s body and those not obtained by either [self or other]:
for those that are with outflows (*sāsrava*), there is only the phrase "severance of the object of cognition" (*ālambana-prahāṇa*);
for those that are without outflows (*anāsrava*), there is the phrase "neither of the two."
Treatise:

Having already explained the acquisition (*prāpti*) of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), this verse summarizes what preceded and introduces what follows. By means of the difference in their acquisitions, their names and essential natures (*svabhāva*) are distinguished.
Treatise:
That which can eternally obstruct [the arising of conditioned phenomena] until they reach their cessation is called "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This explains the verse. As for the statement that "the attainment of cessation is different from the former," it means:
The former was obtained through discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*), whereas this is not obtained through discernment; therefore,
it is said to be different from the former.
That which is attained not through wisdom, but solely due to the absence of conditions, is called "cessation not through deliberation" (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
One should not explain this by saying that its prior cessation is virtuous;
rather, this cessation is neutral (avyākṛta), which distinguishes it from the former.
If that were so, then what was previously obtained as a "wholesome cessation" would now be obtained as "non-wholesome.
Consequently, this newly obtained cessation would differ from the former and should be termed a "non-wholesome cessation."
However, this absence of conditions is called "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
It is obtained through non-deliberative acquisition (*apratisaṃkhyā-prāpti*) and is termed "cessation not through deliberation.
Its designation is explained in the same manner as the previously mentioned "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), following the *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compound analysis.
Treatise:
Attainment does not depend on discernment (pratisaṃkhyā), but arises solely from the deficiency of conditions;
this explains the cause of attainment. According to this treatise, it arises solely from the deficiency of conditions.
That is to say, there is no other power; according to correct reasoning, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* shows that [the cessation of outflows] is obtained through two causes:
first, by the deficiency of conditions;
second, by non-analytical cessation.
Because it is not due to the removal of hindrances through discernment:
if one encounters superior conditions, the phenomenon immediately arises;
if one encounters inferior conditions, the phenomenon does not arise.
The *Nyāya* states:
"Discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*) refers to the wisdom accomplished through diligent application in accordance with reality;
it is not by means of this wisdom [that [cessation occurs]...]"
There is a dharma that eternally obstructs the arising of future dharmas, which is called non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). ... up to ...
if a dharma can obstruct the functional activity of another dharma’s arising, this dharma necessarily obstructs that dharma independently of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Because it causes [the dharma] to abide in the future so that it never arises again, one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
That this dharma is substantially real will be established later. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states:
It is not the case that [a phenomenon] will never arise again simply because its conditions are lacking,
for it should arise again later when it encounters conditions of a similar kind;
such is the detailed meaning of this treatise.
All non-arising occurs due to two conditions:
first, due to the deficiency of conditions;
second, due to analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
As for the claim that "if one later encounters conditions of a similar kind,
the phenomenon can arise," this selection is irrational;
for that subsequent encounter with conditions of a similar kind constitutes the very condition for its arising.
If that which follows is not a condition for arising,
then if there were no deficiency in the preceding conditions for the subsequent arising,
how could it arise if the subsequent [moment] is not a condition?
Because phenomena do not arise due to the absence of conditions, they never arise;
what, then, does the power of cessation have to do with it? [Response: The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states:
"A phenomenon does not [cease] merely through the deficiency of conditions."
This treatise states that it is solely due to the deficiency of conditions;
since the two treatises differ, which is correct?
The answer is: according to the explanation in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, the attainment [of the fruit] differs accordingly.

Conditioned phenomena of the three natures (trisvabhāva) share the same acquisition (*prāpti*) for the purpose of determining their nature, because the power of the acquired phenomenon causes that acquisition to arise.
The acquisition of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) arises from the Path, because it originates based on the Path.
The acquisition of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) arises from the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*).
Because they arise based on the homogeneous class (*sabhāgatā*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is considered useless;
thus, the two types of cessation (*nirodha*) are not determined by what has been acquired (*prāpti*). The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* also states: [text continues].

Since space and the like are useless [for this purpose], we know that this treatise [asserts] that it is merely by the superiority of the principle of the deficiency of conditions [that they are so designated]. Question:
If that is so, why does the *Vibhāṣā* state that "space is a proximate dominant condition (*upādāna-pratyaya*) for the four great elements and so forth"?
Answer: Space is unimpeded, whereas the great elements are impeded;
therefore, they are said to be "near."
It is not meant that being possessed of power constitutes "proximity. Question:
If that is so, why does the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 32, state:
"This non-analytical cessation..."
It is acquired only with respect to dharmas that will not arise in the future. Why is this?
Because this [acquisition] is cessation.
The original intention was to prevent conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) from ever arising again;
if they were never to arise, this acquisition (*prāpti*) would indeed arise.
It is like the acquisition of a phenomenon that is subject to desire, which is bound to a sentient being.
It is being practiced in the present;
it has been practiced in the past;
and it will be practiced in the future.
Since all [conditioned phenomena] possess the characteristic of arising, would it not follow that this cessation cannot apply to those phenomena?
Answer: Although the original intent was to negate conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), [the argument still holds].
As for the method of granting consent (*chanda*),
this is a figurative expression and not literal;
it is because, just as analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) fundamentally intends to exclude contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*).
When dharmas are bound by afflictions,
if they are separated from those bonds,
it is like the case of dharmas associated with desire.
And [the non-arising] is acquired through cessation;
however, this acquisition of cessation results from the power of the path of abandonment, not from analytical cessation itself.
The meaning of the acquisition of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is also to be understood accordingly. If it were not so,
then this non-analytical cessation—
One should attain it for oneself;
this is its efficacious power,
which not only does not obstruct, but [furthermore...]
Some say: "The purpose of this dharma is fundamentally to obstruct dharmas from arising;
if dharmas do not arise, one then immediately gives rise to [this dharma] and transmits it to the practitioner. This interpretation is erroneous.
One should say that dharmas which will never arise obtain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

One should not say that non-analytical cessation has the power to send attainment (*prāpti*) to the practitioner. Since these two explanations are contradictory, one should rely on this treatise. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 32, states:
Question: Regarding the state of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*), is it acquired collectively by all sentient beings, or is it acquired individually?
Answer: This is not fixed.
Regarding the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) of shared phenomena, it is attained collectively;
regarding the non-analytical cessation of unshared phenomena, it is attained individually.
According to the Master of the Evaluation (*viniścayakāra*), one who speaks thus should state it in this manner.
Non-analytical cessation is more numerous;
analytical cessation is less so. Why is this?
Because non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is equal in number to conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma),
whereas analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is equal in number only to contaminated phenomena (sāsrava-dharma);
for if it were otherwise, [it would not be so].

Regarding all phenomena that are subject to arising, if they do not arise despite having the conditions for doing so, they would not attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). According to this scriptural passage, all external objects possess non-analytical cessation.
All of these can be realized.
However, among them there are those that are common and those that are uncommon;
if they are common, they are attained in common.
As with shared property and the like;

if it is not shared, then one attains it individually. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* asks: "By means of the path of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*), one attains the non-arising of afflictions (*kleśa*) and the analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding various places of birth."
Why is it not the fruit of the path?
The answer is:
because one does not cultivate the path for the sake of this cessation.
That is to say, one diligently cultivates the path for the sake of nirvāṇa and for the sake of detachment from defilement.
By means of cultivating the path, one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding the evil destinies and so forth.
If one cultivates the path for the sake of this cessation, [it is called "the path of abandonment"].

One cannot attain this cessation within the evil destinies and so forth; for it is not the case that one who lacks deep revulsion toward saṃsāra can attain non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) regarding the evil destinies.

Therefore, the attainment of non-analytical cessation is not designated as a fruit of the Path. Commentary: This is because one cannot attain this cessation while remaining in the states of miserable rebirth. Since it is impossible for one who does not deeply loathe cyclic existence to attain non-analytical cessation with respect to those miserable realms, the attainment of such cessation is not reckoned as a fruit of the Path.
One seeks the attainment of analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) to attain nirvāṇa;
through profound revulsion toward defiled phenomena, one enters the state of the noble ones (ārya) by permanently severing them.
This is because one may also attain the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) of the miserable destinies (apāya).
If one seeks non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha),
one cannot attain the non-analytical cessation of not being born in the evil destinies;
for because the mind of revulsion is weak, one may later fall back from it.
The statement that one feels aversion toward the miserable realms (*durgati*) implies that one does not feel aversion toward humans or devas;
therefore, the mind of aversion is inferior. Thus says the *Śāstra*.
"Like the eye and the mind attaining non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)" is an explanation by way of citing a specific instance.
"When the eye and the mind are focused on a single form" means that "eye" refers to the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*).
This refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
That is to say, when a portion of the mental consciousness apprehends a visible form (*rūpa*), the other cognitions and associated dharmas attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
Or, it may refer to the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) itself.
When explained by means of mental designations, or when one is focused exclusively on a color such as blue,
at that time colors such as yellow and so forth,
as well as the four objects, perish moment by moment.
The dharmas such as the five consciousnesses that are capable of taking those objects as their spheres abide in the future and will never arise,
because they are incapable of taking the past as their object.
Furthermore, it is because [the mind] can no longer take other objects as its focal point.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"For example, when the eye and the mental faculty are both focused exclusively on a single form..."
Regarding the remaining forms, as well as all sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and so forth,
which perish moment by moment,
the mind takes a small portion of them as its object.
And regarding the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*),
one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) with respect to the five groups of consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya*) and a portion of the mental consciousness (*manovijñānakāya*).
It can never arise with respect to an object that has already ceased,
because it takes a simultaneous object as its condition.
Commentary states:
One portion of the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is such as the eight bases of mastery (aṣṭāv abhibhvāyatanāni) and so forth;
it takes only present objects as its cognitive domain and does not take past objects.
Furthermore, because their objects of perception are fixed, they attain cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This refers to the sense-sphere of mind (*manāyatana*) and the sense-sphere of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
The mind (manas) refers to the various consciousnesses;
the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) consists of mental factors (caitta),
as well as the four characteristics and so forth.
Treatise:
Regarding the attainment of cessation with respect to dharmas that have passed, are present, or are arising—
this constitutes the formal classification for analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
If one examines the cessation of existence and non-existence according to the Dharma:
all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) each have analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),
and all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) each have non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
That is to say, non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is broad,
while analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is narrow.
This is a case of asking about the narrow based on the broad.
To answer by citing the subsequent term when asked about the broad based on the narrow;

to answer by citing the preceding term when asked about the narrow based on the broad. Regarding the attainment through realization (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*), its scope is broad while its essence is narrow.
Because it extends across the three periods of time, its temporal scope is broad;

because it exists only as a contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomenon, its ontological substance is narrow. Non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), however, has a narrow temporal scope but a broad ontological substance:
its temporal scope is narrow because it is acquired only in the future.
Because "all conditioned phenomena" (sarvasaṃskṛta) is broad in scope,
these [categories] differ from it, forming four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
This may be understood according to the text.

the three preceding verses have collectively clarified the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
The following twenty-two verses are divided into the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).

subsequently, they are divided into the bases and elements. The first two verses provide a general explanation of the five aggregates.

The next verse specifically clarifies the contaminated aggregates (*sāsrava-skandha*).

first the conclusion of the previous section introduces the subsequent question, followed by the presentation of the verse as the answer.

this is the first [section].

Next, the verse is cited as a response.
Within it,
the first two lines reiterate the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
