The seventh [section] is the summary.
This enumeration of the names of the aggregates (*skandha*) reveals the essential nature of the name "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*).
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
Because they are concealed, accumulated, impaired, and suppressed by various calamities such as old age, sickness, and death, they are called "aggregates" (skandha).
This explains that conditioned phenomena possess many faults and contradictions.
Hidden within these, they arise whenever conditions meet them,
like thieves lurking in the mountains.
To distinguish them from the other aggregates (skandhas), it is subsequently stated that they consist of "form" (rūpa) and so forth.
The five aggregates beginning with morality cannot fully encompass all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
The five aggregates beginning with form (*rūpa*) do fully encompass conditioned phenomena.
Treatise.
The gathering of various conditions— such as milk or firewood—
explains the nature of the conditioned; there is not even the slightest phenomenon that exists independently.
Since it is produced by conditions,
it has the meaning of being a joint product of various conditions.
If that is so, then regarding future arising and non-arising:
"It should not be conditioned (*saṃskṛta*);
because it belongs to that same category, there is no obstacle to its being in the future.
This is the explanation that resolves the objection.
"Like milk, firewood, and so forth.
This is an illustration.
The *Nyāyabindu* states:
How can that which has not yet arisen in the future be called conditioned?
Because it belongs to that same category,
it is also termed "conditioned," just as firewood is so called even while in its unburnt state.
Because it belongs to that same category, it is also called "fuel.
Alternatively, there is no error in establishing a name based on what has been or what will be,
just as lutes, harps, and the like are said to "possess sound."
Furthermore, just as breasts, lotus ponds, and so forth are non-arising phenomena (*anutpattidharma*),
they are nonetheless called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) because they do not transcend that category.
Treatise.
Because these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) reach the point of being swallowed up [by time],
it explains the "paths of the world" (*adhvan*).
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
Regarding these conditioned phenomena,
in various sūtras,
the Blessed One [has said]:
They are called "worldly paths" (*lokamārga*) and so forth according to their meaning. What, then, are they?
It is said that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are also called "worldly paths."
Because the five aggregates, such as form, are phenomena subject to arising and ceasing,
they circulate through the paths of the future, present, and past.
Regarding those dharmas that do not arise because their various conditions are lacking:
although they do not arise,
there is no error in establishing the name for them, as they belong to that same category.
Some say that because it is swallowed by impermanence, it is called a "world-path" (*adhvan*). According to this, the previous explanation—
that the three times themselves are the path— is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound,
meaning "the path that is the world."
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are called "world-roads" (*adhvan*) because they proceed along the road of the world;
that is, because they possess a world-road, they are called "world-roads.
This is a *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compound. According to the latter explanation, they are so called because they are swallowed by impermanence.
The *Paramārtha-ṭīkā* states:
"Practicing practice without ceasing can exhaust a road of ten thousand *li*;
impermanence is the world."
Conditioned phenomena are the path.
Because they serve as the path for the world, they are called the "world-path";
that is, the path of the world.
This is an *uttarapadalopa* (dependent determinative) compound.
The treatise states:
"Alternatively, it is called the 'basis of names' (*nāma-āśraya*)"; this explains that the basis of speech consists of both the name and its meaning. "Speech" refers to verbal expression.

This refers to the specific differentiation within the continuity of vocal sounds. That which is the basis for this—the so-called "name" (nāma) together with its "meaning" (artha)—serves as the support for speech;
that is, it is the name itself.

Regarding the meaning of "simultaneous": conditioned phenomena may be called "co-existent" across the three time periods, as they can all be described simultaneously as belonging to the past, present, and future; unconditioned phenomena are not like this.
Therefore, [the term "basis of speech"] applies universally to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) but does not extend to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Regarding this, some commentators explain that all conditioned phenomena can be associated with speech and are thus called the "basis of speech.
Accordingly, Venerable Pārśva states in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 15: [text follows].
Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) can coexist with verbal expression; therefore, they are established as the basis of speech (*vāg-āśraya*).
Unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are not so, and for this reason they are not so described. According to this treatise, such is the case.
This refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*),
which share with words the property of falling within the three time periods.
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
As stated in the sutra, there are three bases;
there are not four, nor five. It is according to this that [the teaching] is established.

Although it is taught that [the three times] exist, or alternatively, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) may be said to coexist with their names; because they arise simultaneously with words, they are called the "basis of name and word" (*nāmakāya*). In this regard, there is no difference between this [position] and that of the Venerable [Vasumitra] in the *Abhidharmakośa*.
Treatise:
Such statements rely upon conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
This is because all conditioned phenomena are designated as "co-arising" throughout the three periods of time.
The treatise states that this fully encompasses all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
Otherwise, they would not be included within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
If it were not explained in this way, it would not encompass all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
According to the position of other masters, who maintain that "basis" (*āśraya*) refers only to "name" (*nāman*),
it would fail to include the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
This contradicts what is stated in the treatises regarding the eighteen *dhātus*. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"The basis of speech refers to names (*nāman*)."
The meaning of "all" (sarva) is that it fully encompasses the five aggregates (pañca-skandha),
as stated in the Sūtra.
There are three bases of speech; there are neither four nor five.

By this, the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* is well-explained, for it states that the bases of speech are subsumed within the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). This treatise and the *Nyāyānusāra* likewise cite the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* in this regard.
For what reason does this treatise speak of the eighteen *dhātus*,
while the *Nyāya* speaks of the five *skandhas*?
The *Nyāyānusāra* states that it "comprehensively includes the five aggregates," while this treatise states that it "comprehensively includes all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
Although the phrasing differs slightly, the meaning is the same.
The meaning is no different. Furthermore, refuting the statement of other masters that the "basis of speech" (*vāg-āśraya*) is merely a name, the *Prakaraṇapāda* states:
"The basis of speech is subsumed within the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements. The *Nyāyānusāra* cites the former [the *Prakaraṇapāda*].
In this treatise, citing [the sūtras] later, there is no fault in the meaning;
however, all of them prove that it universally encompasses conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*). Regarding this, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* presents two views.
One view holds that the name is the basis for speech,
while the meaning is the successive basis for speech.
Another view holds that both the name and the meaning are the bases for speech.
This treatise agrees with what is stated later:
that it is only through names (*nāman*) that meanings can be expressed.

When one wishes to speak, one relies upon both [names and phrases]. Question: Why is it said only that [the mind] is associated with names (*nāma-sahita*), and not mentioned as being associated with phrases (*pada*) and so forth?
Answer: At the time of uttering a word, if it merely invokes a phenomenon, there is only the name;
if it includes a distinction, then both name and phrase are present.
Because "name" (nāma) is universal, it is called by that name. Question: If that is so, then "phrasing" (vyañjana) is most universal;
why is it not mentioned?
Answer: Phrasing is the basis [upon which names depend].
However, because it cannot express its own nature or its specific distinctions, it is not so described.

The *Śāstra* states that there is "separation" (*viveka*). The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* says:

"Alternatively, it is called 'possessing separation' (*saviveka*), because [beings] are submerged in the cycle of rebirth within the various realms of existence (*gati*) and transmigrate through birth and death."
Nirvāṇa is called "with departure" because it involves the relinquishing [of existence];
it signifies the cessation of the constant transmigration through the various realms of rebirth.
Once it has been attained, one will certainly not return.
Because this possesses transcendence, it is called "possessing transcendence.
Just as one who possesses wealth is called "wealthy," so too does the conditioned possess the sense of transcendence.
All conditioned phenomena are alike a boat or raft; therefore, even the Noble Path should be relinquished.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Even dharmas should be relinquished."
How much more so regarding what is not the Dharma? According to the commentaries on the two treatises, "nirvāṇa" means eternal detachment;
because all conditioned phenomena possess this detachment [from suffering].
It is called "possessing detachment.
This existence is nirvāṇa;
it is distinct from all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
Because at the time of nirvana all [conditioned things] can be relinquished.
This is not like disjunction (*visamyoga*), which exists only as something contaminated (*sāsrava*).
Within this [category of non-contaminated conditioned phenomena], there is that which is dissociated from all conditioned things (*saṃskṛta*).
At the time of attaining nirvana, all [defilements] can be relinquished;
this is precisely the nirvana that possesses the capacity for relinquishment.

This explains "possessing an object":
because it possesses a cause.
"Thing" (*vastu*) has the meaning of "cause.
Thus, the *Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā* states:
"A thing refers to that which serves as a basis (*āśraya*)."
Alternatively, "that which is inhabited" (or "the locus") has the meaning of "cause," because the effect depends upon the cause and arises from it—
just as a child depends upon its mother— or because the effect can obscure the cause.
It is like a person sitting on a bed;
this is in the sense of being obscured by the fruit,
because the cause and the fruit exist in a temporal sequence of before and after.
Furthermore, because it possesses both subtle and coarse natures, and because it has an objective basis (*vastu*), it is said to be "with objective basis" (*savastuka*).
This is as explained previously; this is according to the interpretation of the two treatises.
The cause is termed "the thing" (vastu).
Because the effect possesses a cause, it is termed "possessing a thing" (savastuka).
All conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta) possess their causes.
Thus, it also encompasses all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*); this is the traditional teaching (*āgama*) of the Vaibhāṣika masters.
However, the Sautrāntika school explains that the term "basis" (*vastu*) is not intended to refer to everything designated by the name "cause" (*hetu*).
That which possesses an object is called "having a substantial entity.
All conditioned phenomena possess a substantial entity, whereas unconditioned phenomena lack a substantial entity; thus, "possessing an object" applies exclusively to conditioned phenomena.

Second, the answer to this question: As previously stated,
all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) other than the noble truth of the path (*mārgasatya*) are termed "with outflows" (*sāsrava*).
In this context, what is established in detail? The treatise states:
"It is the establishment of the appropriated aggregates up to the uncontaminated formations.
This is the answer.
Although this was already explained previously,
it is stated again now in order to show that the aggregates of appropriation (*upādānaskandha*) are also called "aggregates" (*skandha*).
There may be those that are merely aggregates (*skandha*) but not aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*).
Because their meaning as a collection of uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) formations is the same, they are both called "aggregates";
however, because they do not arise from clinging, they are not called "aggregates of clinging."
The treatise states:
"Defilements are called 'appropriating aggregates' (upādānaskandha), like a tree bearing flowers and fruit.
This explains the reason for their designation.
Within this, there are three dharmas and metaphors:
the afflictions are called "grasping" (upādāna),
and the aggregates that arise from the afflictions are called "that which is grasped" (upādatta).
Because it arises from grasping (*upādāna*),
it is named after its cause, just as fire made of grass or chaff is named after its material. Because it is bound to grasping,
it is like a king’s minister.
The name is established based on what [the skandhas] belong to. The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* states:
"The aggregates are driven by afflictions;
for example, due to greed and hatred, there arise such things as doubt."
Because it is capable of producing grasping (*upādāna*),
it is like a flower or fruit tree;
it is designated by the name of its fruit.
Treatise:
These contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena are "like those with outflows";
this explains "that which is subject to contention" (*saraṇa*).
There are two meanings of "worldly contention":
first, it provokes and disturbs virtuous people;
second, it causes harm to oneself and others.
Afflictions are likewise twofold:
first, they disturb the category of wholesome qualities;
second, they cause harm to oneself and others.
Therefore, they are called "contentious" (*raṇa*),
because the aggregates (*skandha*) increase in accordance with contention.
— *Śāstra*.
It is also called "suffering" because it contradicts the noble mind (*āryacitta*).
Since these contaminated aggregates (*sāsravaskandha*) are objects of aversion for the noble mind, they contradict the noble mind;
thus, by virtue of contradicting the noble mind, they are designated as suffering. As the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
The five aggregates of clinging are suffering because they are the basis for all forms of oppression,
and because their intrinsic nature is coarse, heavy, and unstable.
The treatise also calls it "origination" (*samudaya*) because it can summon suffering.
These contaminated aggregates (*sāsrava-skandha*) are called "origination" because they serve as the cause of suffering.
The *Śāstra* states:
"It is also called 'the world' (*loka*) because it reaches its limit in opposition [to the supramundane].
This explains that the name "world" refers to the aggregate of outflows (*sāsrava-skandha*). The *Nyāyānusāra* says:
Alternatively, it is called "mundane" (*loka*) because its nature is subject to destruction.
As the Blessed One said:
"Because its nature is subject to destruction, it is called 'mundane'."
If that were so, the Truth of the Path would be mundane. It is not so;
for there is no destruction of a second [moment].

Because the nature of destruction in the Truth of the Path is indeterminate, whereas the nature of destruction in the world is determinate; thus, the second type of destruction is that which possesses an antidote.

It is also called a "station of views" (*dṛṣṭi-sthāna*) because the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase therein.

That which increases in accordance [with its object] is called "increasing accordingly" (anuśaya).

The five views, such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), increase through their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) while abiding therein. Is it not the case that all outflowing (*sāsrava*) afflictions increase [in this way]?
Is it not the case for all views?
Regarding the inclusion [of views] within the outflows (*āsrava*), the grasping (*upādāna*),
and the disputes (*vivāda*): as for the question "Was it not already stated previously?"—
the intent of this question is that the five views are themselves subsumed under the afflictions (*kleśa*).
In the previous explanation regarding the outflows (*āsrava*),
it was already stated that all afflictions (*kleśa*) increase in accordance with them;
and regarding the increase of contention (*raṇa*) by all afflictions, it was already stated that this refers to the various views (*dṛṣṭi*).
Why are the outflows (āsrava) specifically taught as the bases of views?
Because these various views increase and lie dormant (anuśerate) therein.
Although this is the case, those views [do not increase] in all aspects within the phenomena that possess outflows (sāsravadharma).
At all times, its characteristics are without distinction;
it is firmly grasped and immovable.
Because the latent tendencies (anuśaya) increase accordingly, their essence and function become more intense.

To show that the outflows (āsrava) are the basis for the growth of these various views, they should be stated again; this explains the reason for restating the "bases of views" (dṛṣṭisthāna). As for greed, delusion, and doubt, it is not so.
The four meanings, such as "unsurpassed" and "all-seeded," are not like that;
for those [afflictions] such as greed possess the quality of being "all-seeded," yet they do not exist at all times.
Regarding greed and the others, there are various types of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), and impurities (*mala*). They do not differ from the views at all times.
As for "all types," Master Yu Yuan said:
It universally takes the five doors as its object, or it universally takes the six sense-objects as its object;

"all modes" means—
This means that greed, hatred, and pride possess latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), and stains (*mala*), along with all types of faults;
for the higher [categories] necessarily include the lower.
Thus, these are the specific characteristics of the latent dispositions.
Although they cannot arise at all times in every respect,
this is called "not at all times"; yet it is not that there is no distinction.
Although it is the case that both independent ignorance and the ignorance associated with common-characteristic afflictions exist at all times.
However, the ignorance associated with specific-characteristic afflictions does not exist at all times;
nor does the ignorance associated with anger and so forth exist in all modes or at all times.

There is a distinction in their characteristics. Although doubt lacks such a distinction, it does not involve stubborn adherence; thus, doubt is of the nature of a latent tendency (*anuśaya*) rather than a distinct category of affliction (*kleśa*).
It is not associated with other distinct categories of afflictions.
Furthermore, it is not associated with all types of defiled dharmas;
rather, it exists in every way and at all times.
There is no difference in their characteristics;
yet, because they do not cling firmly, there is doubt as to whether suffering exists or does not exist, and so forth.
It is not a rigid adherence, as it differs from a [wrong] view in that it is a latent disposition (*anuśaya*);
it exists in all its modes,
and because it is a universal affliction (*sarvatraga-kleśa*), it exists at all times.

Because it does not correspond with the afflictions of its own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) nor with the defilements of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), there is no distinction in its nature.
This [view] is the view that negates the self as being either annihilated or eternal, and so forth.
Because they are not hesitant, they are not non-firmly attached;

To speak of them separately as "bases of views" (dṛṣṭi-sthāna) is intended to engender revulsion.
